title: Integrated Business Solutions (Final P6)
description: Open-book multidisciplinary case studies for CA Final Paper 6: seven industry cases that mix FR, AFM, audit, direct and indirect tax, corporate law and strategic management, plus a chapter on how to read, plan and answer the paper.

chapters.title: How the IBS Paper Works and How to Answer It
chapters.summary: The Paper 6 pattern, how to read a long multidisciplinary case, how to split four hours, and how to present answers that score.
chapters.lawAsOf: ICAI Paper 6 assessment pattern announced January 2024 (5 cases of 25 marks, attempt any 4, open book, 4 hours)

lesson.heading: What Paper 6 tests
lesson.body:
Paper 6, Integrated Business Solutions (multidisciplinary case study with strategic management), is the last paper of CA Final Group II under the new scheme. It does not add a new subject. It tests whether you can apply what you learnt in the other Final papers to one business at a time, the way a CA in practice or industry would.

| Feature | Pattern |
| --- | --- |
| Marks and duration | 100 marks, 4 hours |
| Book policy | Open book: you may carry printed or handwritten material |
| Structure | 5 case studies of 25 marks each; attempt any 4 |
| Inside each case | Case-based MCQs (about 10 marks) and descriptive questions (about 15 marks), a 40:60 weightage |
| Knowledge base | Financial Reporting, AFM, Advanced Auditing and Professional Ethics, Direct Tax and International Taxation, Indirect Tax, with Strategic Management integrated into the cases |

Company law and allied laws appear through audit and reporting issues: section 143 reporting, section 186 loans, section 188 related party transactions, CSR under section 135, and schemes of arrangement under sections 230-232. Check the latest ICAI announcement before your attempt; the pattern above is the one ICAI has announced for the new scheme.

lesson.heading: Reading a long case
lesson.body:
A case runs to 4-8 pages: a company background, financial tables in annexures, and 5-8 "issues" raised by the CFO, auditor or board. Read in this order:

- Read the questions first (MCQs and descriptives). They tell you which annexures matter.
- Skim the background: industry, listed or unlisted, Ind AS or AS, holding structure, year end.
- Tag each paragraph in the margin with its subject: FR, AFM, AUD, DT, IDT, LAW, SM. One paragraph often carries two tags (an import of machinery is AFM for the hedge and IDT for customs and IGST credit).
- Circle every figure the questions need and note its unit (₹ crore vs ₹ lakh, USD million).
- Note dates: year end, date of event, appointed date, days overdue. Many answers turn on a date.

Case selection: in the first 15 minutes skim all five cases and drop the one with the most unfamiliar subject mix, not the longest one.

lesson.heading: Time plan for four hours
lesson.body:
Marks per minute decide the plan: 100 marks in 240 minutes is about 0.42 marks per minute, so a 2-mark MCQ is worth under 5 minutes.

| Block | Minutes |
| --- | --- |
| Skim all 5 cases and choose 4 | 15 |
| Case 1 to Case 4 (about 54 minutes each) | 215 |
| Final review: MCQ answers marked, units, conclusions | 10 |
| **Total** | **240** |

Within one case of about 54 minutes: 10 minutes to read and tag, 12-15 minutes for the MCQs, and the rest for the descriptive parts. Answer the MCQs of a case while its facts are fresh. If a computation is not converging after 8 minutes, write the approach and the formula, state an assumption and move on; partial marks are given for the correct method.

lesson.heading: Presenting descriptive answers
lesson.body:
Examiners mark for the right issue, the right provision and a clear conclusion. Use this frame for every descriptive part:

- **Issue**: one line on what is being decided.
- **Provision**: name the standard, section or concept (Ind AS 115, SA 570, section 186 of the Companies Act, the concessional regime for domestic companies corresponding to section 115BAA of the 1961 Act).
- **Analysis**: apply the facts of the case, with working notes in a table.
- **Conclusion**: the answer to the question asked, with the figure and its unit.

Strategy questions (SM) score when you name a framework (SWOT, Porter's five forces, Ansoff, BCG, value chain, balanced scorecard) and apply it to the company's facts. A generic list of SWOT words with no link to the case scores little.

Open book is a trap if you rely on it: there is no time to read a chapter in the hall. Carry a slim index of standards, sections and formats you have already practised.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Writing everything you know about a standard instead of applying it to the case facts.
- Mixing units: the case gives ₹ crore in one annexure and ₹ lakh in another.
- Ignoring the date: an event after the year end is an Ind AS 10 question, not a current year transaction.
- Answering from the old law: the Income-tax Act 2025 uses "tax year" and new section numbers; cite the provision by name and, if unsure of the new number, give the 1961 Act section it corresponds to.
- Spending 20 minutes on a 4-mark part, then rushing the fourth case.
- Leaving MCQs blank: there is no negative marking.

keyPoints: Paper 6: 100 marks, 4 hours, open book, 5 cases of 25 marks, attempt any 4.
Each case: about 10 marks MCQs and 15 marks descriptive (40:60 weightage).
Read the questions first, then tag paragraphs by subject: FR, AFM, AUD, DT, IDT, LAW, SM.
Budget about 54 minutes per case after 15 minutes of selection and 10 minutes of review.
Descriptive frame: issue, provision, analysis with working notes, conclusion with figure and unit.
SM answers score when a named framework is applied to the case facts.

cases.title: Case: Saffron Textiles Ltd (practice reading)
cases.body:
Saffron Textiles Ltd (STL) is a listed Ind AS company in Surat making polyester yarn and fabric. It has opted for the concessional tax regime for domestic companies (22% plus 10% surcharge and 4% cess, an effective rate of 25.168%). Extract of results for FY 2026-27:

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue from operations | 480 |
| EBITDA | 72 |
| Depreciation | 20 |
| Finance cost | 18 |
| Profit before tax | 34 |

Issues raised at the March 2027 board meeting:

- STL will import an air-jet loom line from Japan for USD 5 million, payable three months after shipment.
- A garment exporter owes STL ₹6 crore, overdue for 200 days. It has filed for insolvency.
- The board wants to enter technical textiles (airbags and medical fabrics), products STL has never made, sold to automotive and hospital buyers it has never served.
- An independent director resigned in February 2027, citing concerns about related party purchases from a promoter firm.

questions.prompt: Under the new scheme, how many of the five case studies in Paper 6 must a candidate answer?
options: All five, 20 marks each
Any four, 25 marks each
Any three, 33 marks each
Two compulsory and two of the remaining three
questions.explanation: ICAI's pattern for Paper 6 gives five case studies of 25 marks each, of which any four are answered, for 100 marks in four hours.

questions.prompt: Within a 25-mark case, how are marks split between MCQs and descriptive questions under the announced pattern?
options: About 10 marks MCQ and 15 marks descriptive
About 15 marks MCQ and 10 marks descriptive
25 marks descriptive, no MCQs
About 5 marks MCQ and 20 marks descriptive
questions.explanation: ICAI announced a 40:60 weightage between MCQs and descriptive questions; 40% of 25 is 10 marks of MCQs (typically five MCQs of 2 marks) and 15 marks of descriptive parts.

questions.prompt: Because Paper 6 is open book, a candidate can rely on looking up standards and sections in the hall instead of practising them beforehand.
questions.explanation: At about 54 minutes per case there is no time to learn a provision in the hall. Open book helps you confirm a section number or a format you already know; it does not replace preparation.

questions.prompt: A candidate keeps 15 minutes to skim and choose cases and 10 minutes for final review out of the 240 minutes. How many minutes are left for each of the four cases? Round to the nearest minute.
questions.explanation: Time for cases = 240 - 15 - 10 = 215 minutes. Per case = 215 / 4 = 53.75 minutes, about **54 minutes**.

questions.prompt: Select the statements that correctly describe Paper 6.
options: Strategic Management is integrated into the case studies
The cases draw on FR, AFM, audit, direct tax and indirect tax
Candidates may carry study material into the exam hall
Each case is restricted to a single subject
MCQs carry negative marking
questions.explanation: Paper 6 is multidisciplinary: one case mixes FR, AFM, audit, direct and indirect tax and strategy, and it is open book. Cases are not single-subject and ICAI MCQs carry no negative marking.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: Paper 6 is an ___ book examination.
questions.explanation: Paper 6 is an open-book, case-study-based paper of four hours.

questions.prompt: In Ansoff's matrix, the move into technical textiles is best described as:
options: Market penetration
Market development
Product development
Diversification (related)
questions.explanation: Airbags and medical fabrics are new products for STL, sold to new customer groups (automotive and hospitals). New product plus new market is diversification; it is related because it uses STL's existing fibre and weaving know-how.

questions.prompt: Compute STL's current tax expense on the profit before tax shown, assuming taxable income equals PBT. Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: Tax = 34 x 25.168% = 8.55712, about **₹8.56 crore**. The effective rate is 22% x 1.10 (surcharge) x 1.04 (cess) = 25.168%.

questions.prompt: How should STL treat the ₹6 crore receivable from the garment exporter under Ind AS 109?
options: No allowance until the insolvency process ends
12-month ECL only, as trade receivables are short term
Lifetime ECL, treating the receivable as credit-impaired
Write back the revenue originally recognised
questions.explanation: Trade receivables without a significant financing component use the simplified approach (lifetime ECL always). With 200 days overdue and insolvency filed, the receivable is credit-impaired; measure lifetime ECL on the expected recoveries. Revenue is not reversed: the sale was valid when made.

questions.prompt: Which pair of subjects does the loom import issue mainly test?
options: AFM (forex exposure and hedging) and indirect tax (customs duty and IGST credit)
Audit and corporate law only
Direct tax only
Strategic management only
questions.explanation: A USD payable three months later is a transaction exposure to hedge (AFM). The import attracts basic customs duty and IGST, and the IGST is available as input tax credit (indirect tax). The capitalised cost also matters for FR and tax depreciation, but the main tags are AFM and IDT.

questions.prompt: Compute STL's interest coverage ratio as EBITDA divided by finance cost. Answer in times to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: Interest coverage = EBITDA / finance cost = 72 / 18 = **4.00 times**.

questions.prompt: Prepare an answer plan for the Saffron Textiles practice case: tag each of the four issues with subjects and the provision or framework you would cite, and allocate your 54 minutes.
questions.answer:
| Issue | Subjects | Provision or framework |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loom import USD 5 million | AFM, IDT, FR | Forward cover vs money market hedge; customs duty and IGST credit; Ind AS 16 cost and Ind AS 21 for the payable |
| ₹6 crore overdue receivable | FR, AUD | Ind AS 109 simplified approach, credit-impaired; SA 540 for the estimate |
| Technical textiles | SM | Ansoff (related diversification), SWOT, Porter's five forces of the new industry |
| Independent director resignation | LAW, AUD | SEBI LODR disclosure of reasons; section 188 and Ind AS 24 for promoter purchases; SA 550 related parties |

Time plan (54 minutes): read and tag 10, MCQs 14, descriptive parts 26 (by marks), review 4.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate read and approach a long multidisciplinary case in Paper 6?
questions.answer:
- Read the questions first so you know which annexures and figures matter.
- Skim the background for the facts that change the answer: Ind AS or AS, listed or unlisted, year end, tax regime, holding structure.
- Tag each paragraph by subject (FR, AFM, AUD, DT, IDT, LAW, SM); one issue can carry two tags.
- Circle figures with units and dates (overdue days, appointed date, put-to-use date).
- Answer MCQs of the case while the facts are fresh, then the descriptive parts in order of marks.
- Keep to about 54 minutes per case; write the method and an assumption when a computation stalls.

questions.prompt: What makes a descriptive answer in Paper 6 score well?
questions.answer: A scoring answer follows issue, provision, analysis, conclusion. It names the exact standard or section (for example Ind AS 115 on variable consideration, SA 701 for key audit matters, section 186 of the Companies Act), applies it to the case facts with a working note table, and ends with a clear conclusion including the figure and unit. For strategy, it names a framework and applies it to the company. It states assumptions where the case is silent, cites the Income-tax Act 2025 provision by name (with the 1961 section it corresponds to if the new number is uncertain), and avoids reproducing theory that the question does not ask for.

chapters.title: Case Set: Manufacturing (Auto Components)
chapters.summary: A capacity expansion at a listed auto component maker: WACC, NPV, import hedging, Ind AS 16 and 23, customs and IGST credit, tax depreciation, section 186, fraud reporting and the EV threat.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA; Companies Act 2013; SAs issued by ICAI; Income-tax Act 2025 (tax year 2026-27, Finance Act 2026); CGST/IGST Acts after the September 2025 rate rationalisation

lesson.heading: Capex decisions: WACC and NPV
lesson.body:
A manufacturing case almost always contains a capex proposal. The AFM part asks for the discount rate and the NPV; the SM part asks whether the project fits the strategy.

- Cost of equity by CAPM: Ke = Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf).
- Post-tax cost of debt: Kd x (1 - t). For a company in the concessional regime t = 25.168%.
- WACC uses market value weights where the case gives them.
- NPV = PV of incremental post-tax cash flows (including post-tax salvage and working capital release) - initial outlay.

A negative NPV does not end the answer. If the project protects the core business or opens a new market (an EV line for an engine-parts maker), discuss the real option: the right to expand later has value that a single NPV misses. Say whether the strategic value plausibly exceeds the negative NPV.

lesson.heading: Cost of an imported machine: Ind AS 16, Ind AS 23 and customs
lesson.body:
Cost of property, plant and equipment (Ind AS 16) = purchase price + non-refundable import duties + directly attributable costs (installation, testing, professional fees). Recoverable taxes such as IGST for which input tax credit is taken are excluded.

Customs on import (rates are given in the case; use them):

| Item | Base |
| --- | --- |
| Assessable value | CIF value at the CBIC notified exchange rate |
| Basic customs duty (BCD) | % of assessable value |
| Social welfare surcharge (SWS) | 10% of BCD |
| IGST | % of (assessable value + BCD + SWS) |

BCD and SWS are costs. IGST paid on import is available as input tax credit on capital goods, unless the company claims tax depreciation on the IGST component (section 16(3) of the CGST Act bars both).

Ind AS 23: borrowing costs on a qualifying asset are capitalised from commencement (expenditure incurred, borrowing costs incurred and activities started) until the asset is substantially ready. For specific borrowings, capitalise actual cost less investment income on temporary investment of unused funds.

lesson.heading: Tax depreciation and the concessional regime
lesson.body:
Under the Income-tax Act 2025 the block of assets method continues. Two points are tested again and again:

- An asset put to use for less than 180 days in the tax year gets half the normal rate (plant and machinery: 7.5% instead of 15%).
- A company in the concessional regime (corresponds to section 115BAA of the 1961 Act, 22% base rate) cannot claim additional depreciation on new plant (corresponds to section 32(1)(iia)).

Actual cost for tax excludes the GST credit taken. Interest on a loan for the asset up to the date it is first put to use is added to actual cost, and later interest is a revenue deduction.

lesson.heading: Audit and company law issues in a plant case
lesson.body:
- **Inventory**: slow-moving dies and spares are written down to NRV (Ind AS 2). The auditor attends the count (SA 501) and tests ageing.
- **Loans to group companies (section 186)**: limit is the higher of 60% of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium, or 100% of free reserves and securities premium. Above the limit a special resolution is needed. A loan to a wholly owned subsidiary is exempt from the limit and special resolution under the proviso to section 186(3), but the board resolution with consent of all directors present (section 186(5)), disclosure in the financial statements (section 186(4)) and the register still apply.
- **Fraud (section 143(12))**: fraud by officers or employees of ₹1 crore or more is reported by the auditor to the Central Government; below ₹1 crore it is reported to the audit committee or board and disclosed in the Board's report.
- **Key audit matters (SA 701)**: for a listed company, a large capitalisation project is a typical KAM.

lesson.heading: Strategy: the auto component industry
lesson.body:
Porter's five forces in auto components: buyer power is high (a few OEMs buy most of the output and demand annual price cuts), supplier power is moderate (steel and aluminium are commodities), rivalry is intense, and the threat of substitutes is rising because EVs remove engine and transmission parts. A company that makes ICE parts faces a strategic drift risk.

Responses to discuss: product development into EV parts (motors, battery housings), cost leadership through automation, a technology joint venture, or diversification into non-auto engineering. Link each option to the case figures: capacity, margin, balance sheet strength.

keyPoints: Ke = Rf + beta x (Rm - Rf); Kd post-tax = Kd x (1 - 25.168%) under the concessional regime.
Ind AS 16 cost includes BCD and SWS but excludes IGST credited.
Ind AS 23: capitalise specific borrowing cost from commencement to ready date, less temporary investment income.
Tax: half rate if used under 180 days; no additional depreciation in the concessional regime.
Section 186: loan to a wholly owned subsidiary needs no special resolution, but board approval and disclosure still apply.
Section 143(12): fraud of ₹1 crore or more goes to the Central Government.

cases.title: Case: Vardhan Auto Components Ltd - EV line expansion
cases.body:
Vardhan Auto Components Ltd (VACL) is a listed Ind AS company in Pune. About 70% of its revenue comes from engine and transmission parts sold to four passenger-vehicle OEMs. It has opted for the concessional tax regime (effective rate 25.168%).

| Extract, FY 2025-26 | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue | 1,200 |
| EBITDA | 168 |
| Market capitalisation | 1,600 |
| Debt (market value) | 400 |

The board is evaluating an EV component line (motor housings and battery trays) costing ₹150 crore. Expected incremental post-tax cash flows (₹ crore): Year 1: 30, Year 2: 40, Year 3: 45, Year 4: 45, Year 5: 40, plus post-tax salvage of 20 at the end of Year 5.

Capital market data: risk-free rate 7%, VACL beta 1.2, market risk premium 7%, pre-tax cost of debt 9.5%. The CFO proposes to use 14% (WACC rounded up) as the hurdle rate.

The main machine is imported from Germany for USD 10 million, payable six months after shipment. Rates: spot ₹88.00/USD, six-month forward ₹89.20/USD, rupee borrowing rate 8% p.a., USD deposit rate 5% p.a.

Two OEM customers have announced that 40% of their models will be electric by 2030 and have asked VACL for a 3% annual price reduction on existing parts.

cases.title: Case: Vardhan Auto Components Ltd - year-end issues FY 2026-27
cases.body:
The following matters arose while finalising VACL's FY 2026-27 accounts and tax computation.

1. **Import and capitalisation.** The German machine arrived in May 2026. Assessable value at the CBIC notified rate: ₹88 crore. Duty rates to be assumed: BCD 7.5%, SWS 10% of BCD, IGST 18%. VACL takes credit of the IGST. Installation and trial run cost ₹4.74 crore (net of GST credit). The machine was put to use on 31 January 2027.
2. **Borrowing.** A specific term loan of ₹100 crore at 9% p.a. was drawn on 1 April 2026. Installation activity and expenditure began on 1 June 2026 and the line was ready for use on 31 January 2027. Unused funds earned ₹0.40 crore in a liquid fund during June 2026 to January 2027.
3. **Inventory.** Dies for a discontinued model carry a cost of ₹14 crore; the scrap value is ₹5 crore.
4. **Loan.** In December 2026 VACL lent ₹60 crore at 8% p.a. to its wholly owned subsidiary VACL Electric Pvt Ltd. Paid-up capital ₹50 crore, free reserves ₹400 crore, securities premium ₹90 crore; existing loans and investments ₹420 crore.
5. **Fraud.** During the audit, the statutory auditor found that a stores manager had diverted scrap sales of ₹1.4 crore over two years.

questions.prompt: Compute VACL's WACC using market value weights. Answer as a % to 2 decimals.
Compute the NPV of the EV line at the 14% hurdle rate. Use discount factors to 4 decimals and answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals (negative if the NPV is negative).
Compute the rupee outflow at the end of six months if VACL uses a money market hedge for the USD 10 million payable. Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
- USD to deposit today = 10,000,000 / (1 + 5% x 6/12) = USD 9.756098 million.
- Rupees borrowed today = 9.756098 million x ₹88 = ₹85.8537 crore.
- Repayment after six months = 85.8537 x (1 + 8% x 6/12) = **₹89.29 crore**.

Forward cover costs 10 million x 89.20 = ₹89.20 crore.

questions.prompt: Which hedge should VACL choose for the import payable and why?
options: Forward cover, because it costs about ₹9 lakh less than the money market hedge
Money market hedge, because borrowing in rupees is always cheaper
Leave it unhedged, because the rupee is expected to appreciate
Forward cover, because it costs about ₹90 lakh less
questions.explanation: Forward outflow ₹89.20 crore vs money market hedge ₹89.29 crore. The forward is cheaper by about ₹8.8 lakh. Leaving a large capex payable unhedged is speculation, not policy.

questions.prompt: Applying Porter's five forces, which force is the strongest pressure on VACL's margins today?
options: Bargaining power of buyers (four OEMs demanding price cuts)
Bargaining power of suppliers of steel
Threat of new entrants, as entry barriers are low
Rivalry from foreign component makers only
questions.explanation: Four OEMs take most of VACL's output and are demanding 3% annual price cuts: concentrated buyers with low switching costs (they can multi-source) have high bargaining power. The EV shift adds a substitute threat over the medium term.

questions.prompt: Compute the borrowing cost VACL should capitalise under Ind AS 23 for FY 2026-27. Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Interest 1 June 2026 to 31 January 2027: 100 x 9% x 8/12 | 6.00 |
| Less: income on temporary investment of unused funds | (0.40) |
| **Capitalised** | **5.60** |

Interest for April-May (before commencement) and February-March (after the asset is ready), ₹1.50 crore each, is charged to profit or loss.

questions.prompt: Compute the IGST paid on import of the machine, which VACL takes as input tax credit. Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Assessable value | 88.00 |
| BCD 7.5% | 6.60 |
| SWS 10% of BCD | 0.66 |
| Value for IGST | 95.26 |
| **IGST 18%** | **17.1468** |

IGST is about ₹17.15 crore. BCD and SWS (₹7.26 crore) are part of cost; IGST credited is not.

questions.prompt: Ignoring interest, the machine's actual cost for tax is ₹100 crore (88 + 6.60 + 0.66 + 4.74). What depreciation can VACL claim on it for tax year 2026-27?
options: ₹7.50 crore: half of 15% as it was used for less than 180 days, and no additional depreciation in the concessional regime
₹15.00 crore: full year rate
₹17.50 crore: 7.5% normal plus 10% additional depreciation
₹35.00 crore: 15% normal plus 20% additional depreciation
questions.explanation: Put to use on 31 January 2027, so fewer than 180 days in the tax year: rate 7.5%. A company in the concessional regime (corresponds to section 115BAA of the 1961 Act) cannot claim additional depreciation. Depreciation = 100 x 7.5% = ₹7.50 crore.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the ₹60 crore loan to VACL Electric Pvt Ltd is correct?
options: No special resolution is needed as the borrower is a wholly owned subsidiary, but a board resolution with consent of all directors present and disclosure in the financial statements are required
A special resolution is mandatory because existing loans and investments exceed 60% of paid-up capital and free reserves
The loan is void because a company cannot lend to its subsidiary
Only the shareholders' ordinary resolution is required
questions.explanation: Limit = higher of 60% x (50 + 400 + 90) = ₹324 crore or 100% x (400 + 90) = ₹490 crore. Even apart from the limit, the proviso to section 186(3) exempts loans to a wholly owned subsidiary from the special resolution. Section 186(5) board approval and section 186(4) disclosure still apply.

questions.prompt: What must the statutory auditor do about the ₹1.4 crore scrap fraud?
options: Report it to the Central Government under section 143(12) after seeking the board's or audit committee's reply within the prescribed time
Only disclose it in the Board's report
Report it to the audit committee only, as it is below ₹5 crore
Ignore it, as management has detected it
questions.explanation: Fraud by an employee of ₹1 crore or more is reported by the auditor to the Central Government. Under the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules the auditor first sends the report to the board or audit committee, considers their reply, and then forwards it with comments to the Central Government within the prescribed time.

questions.prompt: IGST paid on import of a capital asset is included in its Ind AS 16 cost even when the company takes input tax credit of it.
questions.explanation: Ind AS 16 includes only non-refundable taxes. IGST credited is recoverable, so it is excluded from cost. Claiming depreciation on the IGST component while also taking credit is barred by section 16(3) of the CGST Act.

questions.prompt: Which of these form part of the Ind AS 16 cost of a new production line?
options: Basic customs duty on the imported machine
Installation and trial run costs
Borrowing cost on a specific loan during construction (Ind AS 23)
Operating losses in the first three months after the line is ready
Staff training cost on the new line
questions.explanation: Non-refundable duties, directly attributable installation and testing costs, and eligible borrowing costs are capitalised. Initial operating losses and staff training are expensed under Ind AS 16.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a listed company's auditor communicates the most significant matters of the audit, such as a large capitalisation project, as key audit matters under SA ___.
questions.explanation: SA 701, Communicating Key Audit Matters in the Independent Auditor's Report, applies to audits of listed entities and where the auditor decides to communicate KAMs.

questions.prompt: Using the VACL year-end facts, compute the Ind AS 16 cost of the German machine at 31 January 2027 and pass the journal entry for the inventory write-down.
questions.data: Assessable value ₹88 crore; BCD 7.5%; SWS 10% of BCD; IGST 18% (credit taken); installation and trial run ₹4.74 crore; borrowing cost eligible for capitalisation ₹5.60 crore. Dies for a discontinued model: cost ₹14 crore, scrap value ₹5 crore.
questions.answer:
**Cost of machine (Ind AS 16)**

| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Assessable value | 88.00 |
| BCD 7.5% | 6.60 |
| SWS 10% of BCD | 0.66 |
| Installation and trial run | 4.74 |
| Borrowing cost capitalised (Ind AS 23) | 5.60 |
| **Cost** | **105.60** |

IGST of ₹17.15 crore is excluded as credit is taken.

**Inventory write-down (Ind AS 2)**: cost ₹14 crore, NRV ₹5 crore.

| Entry | Dr ₹ crore | Cr ₹ crore |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cost of materials / inventory write-down expense Dr | 9.00 | |
| To Inventory (dies) | | 9.00 |

Disclose the write-down as required by Ind AS 2.

questions.prompt: VACL's EV line shows a negative NPV. Advise the board whether to proceed, combining AFM and strategic analysis.
questions.answer:
- Stand-alone NPV at 14% is about ₹-4.73 crore, so on cash flows alone the project destroys a little value.
- But the base business faces a substitute threat: OEMs plan 40% EV models by 2030, and buyer power is already forcing 3% price cuts. Doing nothing means a shrinking ICE revenue base (strategic drift).
- The EV line is a product development move (Ansoff) and carries a real option: it gives VACL qualification with OEMs for future EV platforms. If the value of that option to expand exceeds about ₹5 crore, the project is worth taking.
- Reduce the gap: negotiate OEM volume commitments, seek PLI-type incentives if eligible, phase the capex, hedge the import at the cheaper forward rate.
- Recommendation: proceed with a phased investment and milestones, and report KPIs (EV revenue share, margin) on a balanced scorecard.

questions.prompt: Explain the auditor's reporting duty on fraud under section 143(12) of the Companies Act 2013.
questions.answer: If the auditor, in the course of audit, has reason to believe that an offence of fraud is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees, the auditor reports it. For fraud of ₹1 crore or more, the auditor sends the report to the board or audit committee seeking their reply within the prescribed time, and then forwards the report with the reply and comments to the Central Government within the prescribed time. Below ₹1 crore, the auditor reports to the audit committee or board, and the company discloses the details in the Board's report. The duty also applies to cost auditors and secretarial auditors. Under SA 240, the auditor also evaluates the effect on the financial statements and on other audit areas.

chapters.title: Case Set: Banking and NBFC
chapters.summary: A middle-layer NBFC: Ind AS 109 staging and ECL, effective interest rate, capital adequacy, duration gap, GST credit for lenders, tax on provisions, NBFC audit reporting and co-lending strategy.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA; Companies Act 2013; SAs issued by ICAI; Income-tax Act 2025 (tax year 2026-27, Finance Act 2026); CGST/IGST Acts after the September 2025 rate rationalisation; RBI scale-based regulation for NBFCs

lesson.heading: Ind AS 109 for lenders: staging and ECL
lesson.body:
An NBFC under Ind AS measures loans at amortised cost (business model: hold to collect; cash flows: solely payments of principal and interest) and books expected credit loss (ECL).

| Stage | Trigger | Allowance | Interest income on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stage 1 | Performing, no significant increase in credit risk (SICR) | 12-month ECL | Gross carrying amount |
| Stage 2 | SICR since initial recognition; rebuttable presumption at more than 30 days past due | Lifetime ECL | Gross carrying amount |
| Stage 3 | Credit-impaired; rebuttable presumption of default at more than 90 days past due | Lifetime ECL | Net carrying amount (gross less allowance) |

Simplified ECL = EAD x PD x LGD, with PD for 12 months in Stage 1 and lifetime PD in Stage 2. In Stage 3 PD is 100%.

**Effective interest rate (EIR)**: processing fees received and directly attributable costs are part of the EIR and amortised over the loan life, not taken to profit on day one.

lesson.heading: Capital adequacy and ALM
lesson.body:
RBI requires NBFCs in the base layer above the deposit threshold and in the middle and upper layers to maintain a capital to risk-weighted assets ratio (CRAR) of at least 15%, with Tier 1 capital of at least 10%.

CRAR = (Tier 1 + Tier 2) / risk-weighted assets x 100.

Asset liability management (AFM link): an NBFC that borrows short and lends long carries interest rate risk.

- Duration gap DGAP = DA - (L / A) x DL.
- Approximate change in equity value: change in E = -DGAP x A x change in rate (ignoring 1 + r, as many exam questions instruct).
- Positive DGAP: equity falls when rates rise. Fix by lengthening liabilities (longer-tenor NCDs) or using interest rate swaps (pay fixed, receive floating).

lesson.heading: Tax and GST for lenders
lesson.body:
**GST**: interest on loans is exempt; processing fees, foreclosure charges and other fee income are taxable (typically 18%). Because the NBFC makes both exempt and taxable supplies, its input tax credit is restricted. Section 17(4) of the CGST Act gives a banking company or financial institution, including an NBFC, the option to avail 50% of eligible ITC every month, the balance lapsing. Credits blocked by section 17(5) are excluded first. The 50% restriction does not apply to tax on supplies from another registered person with the same PAN.

**Income tax**: an ECL allowance is a book provision. It is not deductible as such; the tax computation allows actual bad debts written off and the specific deduction for provisions for bad and doubtful debts available to notified financial entities (corresponds to sections 36(1)(vii) and 36(1)(viia) of the 1961 Act). This creates a deferred tax asset under Ind AS 12 when recovery is probable.

lesson.heading: Audit and regulation of an NBFC
lesson.body:
- An NBFC must hold a certificate of registration under section 45-IA of the RBI Act. CARO 2020 clause 3(xvi) asks the auditor whether the company is required to be registered and has obtained registration.
- RBI directions require the statutory auditor of an NBFC to report additional matters (registration, net owned fund, compliance with prudential norms) and to report exceptions directly to RBI.
- ECL is an accounting estimate with high estimation uncertainty: apply SA 540 (test the model, PD and LGD data, management overlays), and SA 620 if an expert's work is used. ECL is a usual key audit matter (SA 701) for a listed lender.
- Related party loans and evergreening (fresh loans to repay old ones) are classic red flags; test for loans that roll over just before 90 days past due.

lesson.heading: Strategy for a mid-sized NBFC
lesson.body:
Funding cost is the NBFC's main weakness against banks; local underwriting and speed are its strengths. Strategic options commonly examined:

- **Co-lending with banks**: the bank funds most of the loan, the NBFC originates and services it and keeps a minimum share. This is a strategic alliance that lowers the NBFC's funding cost and lets it grow without equivalent capital.
- **Focus strategy** (Porter): niche segments such as used commercial vehicles or rural MSMEs where banks lack reach.
- **Digital lending**: faster processing, but RBI's digital lending rules on disclosures and fund flows apply.

A good answer uses SWOT with the case figures (CRAR headroom, Stage 3 ratio, funding mix) and then recommends one option.

keyPoints: Stage 1: 12-month ECL; Stage 2 (>30 dpd presumption): lifetime ECL; Stage 3 (>90 dpd): lifetime ECL, interest on net amount.
ECL = EAD x PD x LGD; processing fees go into the EIR.
CRAR for NBFC: minimum 15%, Tier 1 at least 10%.
DGAP = DA - (L/A) x DL; change in E = -DGAP x A x change in r.
Section 17(4) CGST: lenders may take 50% of eligible ITC each month; exclude section 17(5) credits first.
ECL is a book provision for tax; deferred tax asset under Ind AS 12.
CARO 3(xvi): registration under section 45-IA of the RBI Act.

cases.title: Case: Kaveri Finserv Ltd - loan book and capital
cases.body:
Kaveri Finserv Ltd (KFL) is a non-deposit-taking NBFC in the middle layer, lending for used commercial vehicles and to small businesses in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. It follows Ind AS and closes its books on 31 March 2027.

**Loan book at 31 March 2027 (₹ crore)**

| Stage | Gross loans (EAD) | PD | LGD |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stage 1 | 4,000 | 1.5% (12-month) | 40% |
| Stage 2 | 600 | 18% (lifetime) | 45% |
| Stage 3 | 250 | 100% | 60% |

Opening ECL allowance was ₹180 crore.

**Capital and ALM data (₹ crore)**

| Item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Tier 1 capital | 900 |
| Tier 2 capital | 150 |
| Risk-weighted assets | 5,600 |
| Total rate-sensitive assets (duration 2.5 years) | 5,000 |
| Total rate-sensitive liabilities (duration 1.8 years) | 4,200 |

The treasury head expects rates to rise by 1% next year. A borrower with a ₹3 crore loan was 45 days past due at year end; another borrower was 95 days past due.

cases.title: Case: Kaveri Finserv Ltd - tax, audit and strategy
cases.body:
Further information for FY 2026-27:

- KFL earns interest income of ₹780 crore and processing and foreclosure fees of ₹42 crore.
- GST paid on inputs and input services during the year: ₹4.20 crore, of which ₹0.30 crore relates to motor cars used by senior staff (blocked under section 17(5)). KFL has opted for the 50% option under section 17(4).
- The board's tax computation adds back the ECL charge for the year.
- The auditors noted that KFL's registration certificate is in order and that two loans to a promoter group firm were renewed every 85 days.
- KFL's average cost of borrowing is 9.8% against 7.5% for large private banks. A private bank has offered a co-lending arrangement in which the bank funds 80% of each loan and KFL funds 20% and services the loan.

questions.prompt: Compute KFL's total ECL allowance required at 31 March 2027. Answer in ₹ crore to 1 decimal.
Compute KFL's CRAR. Answer as a % to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: CRAR = (900 + 150) / 5,600 x 100 = **18.75%**. Tier 1 ratio = 900 / 5,600 = 16.07%. Both exceed the RBI minimums of 15% and 10%.

questions.prompt: Using the duration gap approach (ignore 1 + r), compute the approximate change in the market value of KFL's equity if rates rise by 1%. Answer in ₹ crore to 1 decimal, negative for a fall.
questions.explanation:
DGAP = 2.5 - (4,200 / 5,000) x 1.8 = 2.5 - 1.512 = 0.988 years.

Change in E = -0.988 x 5,000 x 1% = **₹-49.4 crore**. A positive gap means equity value falls when rates rise.

questions.prompt: How should KFL stage the ₹3 crore loan that is 45 days past due, absent other information?
options: Stage 2, with lifetime ECL, as it is more than 30 days past due
Stage 1, as it is less than 90 days past due
Stage 3, as any overdue loan is credit-impaired
Written off, as it is overdue
questions.explanation: Ind AS 109 has a rebuttable presumption that credit risk has increased significantly when payments are more than 30 days past due. The loan moves to Stage 2 (lifetime ECL) but interest is still on the gross amount. Stage 3 applies at more than 90 days past due (the 95-day borrower).

questions.prompt: Which conclusion on KFL's capital position is correct?
options: KFL meets the 15% CRAR and 10% Tier 1 minimums with headroom
KFL breaches CRAR because Tier 2 cannot be counted
KFL breaches the Tier 1 minimum of 18%
CRAR does not apply to non-deposit-taking NBFCs in the middle layer
questions.explanation: CRAR 18.75% is above 15% and Tier 1 16.07% is above 10%. Tier 2 counts (up to the amount of Tier 1). Middle-layer NBFCs are subject to the capital requirement.

questions.prompt: Compute the input tax credit KFL can avail for FY 2026-27 under the 50% option. Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| GST paid on inputs and input services | 4.20 |
| Less: blocked credit on motor cars, section 17(5) | (0.30) |
| Eligible ITC | 3.90 |
| **50% under section 17(4)** | **1.95** |

The other ₹1.95 crore lapses and is a cost.

questions.prompt: How is the ECL charge treated in KFL's income-tax computation?
options: Added back as a book provision; deduction is allowed for actual write-offs and the specific deduction for provisions available to notified financial entities
Fully allowed because it follows Ind AS 109
Allowed only if the auditor certifies the ECL model
Ignored, because NBFCs pay tax on cash profits
questions.explanation: Ind AS provisions are not automatically deductible. The tax law allows bad debts actually written off and a specific deduction for provisions for bad and doubtful debts of certain financial entities (corresponds to sections 36(1)(vii) and 36(1)(viia) of the 1961 Act). The timing difference creates a deferred tax asset under Ind AS 12.

questions.prompt: What does the renewal of the promoter group loans every 85 days most likely indicate to the auditor?
options: Possible evergreening to avoid Stage 3 and NPA classification, requiring testing of the borrower's repayment capacity and related party disclosures
Good collection performance
A routine treasury practice with no audit significance
A GST compliance issue
questions.explanation: Renewing just before 90 days past due can hide credit impairment (evergreening). The auditor applies SA 550 (related parties), SA 540 (ECL estimate) and SA 240 (fraud risk), checks whether fresh funds actually repaid old dues, and considers reporting under the RBI directions.

questions.prompt: In strategic terms, the co-lending offer is best described as:
options: A strategic alliance that lowers KFL's blended funding cost while it keeps origination and customer relationships
Forward integration by KFL into banking
A divestment of KFL's loan book
Cost leadership through scale economies in borrowing
questions.explanation: The bank and KFL combine complementary strengths: the bank's cheap funds and KFL's local reach. KFL funds only 20% of each loan, so its blended funding cost falls and capital goes further. It is a contractual alliance, not integration or divestment.

questions.prompt: Compute the effective interest rate of this loan. Answer as a % to 2 decimals.
questions.data: KFL disburses a one-year bullet loan of ₹10,00,000 at 12% interest payable at maturity with the principal. It collects a processing fee of 2% (₹20,000) upfront, deducted from the disbursement. Ignore GST on the fee.
questions.explanation:
Net amount lent = 10,00,000 - 20,000 = ₹9,80,000. Receipt at maturity = 10,00,000 + 1,20,000 = ₹11,20,000.

EIR = 11,20,000 / 9,80,000 - 1 = **14.29%**. The fee is recognised over the loan life through the EIR, not as income on day one.

questions.prompt: A loan in Stage 2 under Ind AS 109 carries a 12-month ECL allowance because it is still performing.
questions.explanation: Stage 2 loans have had a significant increase in credit risk and carry lifetime ECL. Only Stage 1 uses 12-month ECL. Interest is still computed on the gross carrying amount in Stage 2.

questions.prompt: Which of these are indicators of a significant increase in credit risk for an NBFC borrower?
options: Payments more than 30 days past due
Downgrade of the borrower's external rating
Restructuring of the loan due to the borrower's financial difficulty
An increase in the NBFC's own cost of funds
Borrower opening a new branch with its own funds
questions.explanation: Days past due, rating downgrades and restructuring for financial difficulty all signal deterioration in the borrower's credit risk. The lender's own funding cost and the borrower's expansion from own funds do not.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: an NBFC must obtain a certificate of registration under section ___ of the RBI Act, 1934.
questions.explanation: Section 45-IA of the RBI Act requires registration with RBI before an NBFC commences business. CARO 2020 clause 3(xvi) asks the auditor to report on it.

questions.prompt: Pass the year-end journal entry for KFL's ECL and show the presentation of the loan book in the balance sheet.
questions.data: Gross loans: Stage 1 ₹4,000 crore, Stage 2 ₹600 crore, Stage 3 ₹250 crore. Required ECL: Stage 1 ₹24.0 crore, Stage 2 ₹48.6 crore, Stage 3 ₹150.0 crore. Opening allowance ₹180 crore.
questions.answer:
**Journal entry (₹ crore)**

| Entry | Dr | Cr |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Impairment on financial instruments (P&L) Dr | 42.60 | |
| To ECL allowance on loans | | 42.60 |

Charge = 222.60 - 180.00 = 42.60.

**Presentation (Schedule III, Division III)**

| Loans at amortised cost | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Gross loans (4,000 + 600 + 250) | 4,850.00 |
| Less: impairment loss allowance | (222.60) |
| **Net loans** | **4,627.40** |

Notes disclose the stage-wise movement of gross loans and allowance, the ECL methodology and the Stage 3 ratio (250 / 4,850 = 5.15%).

questions.prompt: What are the key audit considerations in the audit of ECL of an NBFC?
questions.answer:
- Understand the ECL model and governance: staging rules, SICR criteria, definitions of default (SA 315).
- Test data feeding the model: days past due, collateral values, restructuring flags; test IT controls over the loan system.
- Evaluate PD, LGD and EAD assumptions against history and forward-looking information; check management overlays (SA 540, with a retrospective review of last year's estimate).
- Look for evergreening and related party loans (SA 550, SA 240).
- Use an auditor's expert for model validation where needed (SA 620).
- Check Ind AS 107 disclosures and report ECL as a key audit matter for a listed NBFC (SA 701).
- Report the additional matters required by RBI's directions for NBFC auditors and CARO 3(xvi).

questions.prompt: Using SWOT, advise KFL whether to accept the co-lending offer.
questions.answer:
- **Strengths**: local underwriting in used CV and MSME loans, CRAR of 18.75% with headroom.
- **Weaknesses**: borrowing cost 9.8% vs 7.5% for banks; Stage 3 ratio of about 5%.
- **Opportunities**: co-lending lowers the blended cost (80% of each loan funded at bank cost), lets KFL grow faster per rupee of capital and earn servicing income.
- **Threats**: dependence on one bank, sharing of customer data, and the bank's tighter credit criteria may exclude part of KFL's segment.

Recommendation: accept, but negotiate exclusivity limits, a clear servicing fee, and keep a share of non-co-lent business to retain its niche. Track asset quality and funding cost on a balanced scorecard.

chapters.title: Case Set: Infrastructure and Real Estate
chapters.summary: An EPC and real estate developer: Ind AS 115 over-time revenue, onerous contracts, DSCR covenants, RERA escrow, GST on under-construction flats, stamp duty value rules, section 186 for infrastructure companies and going concern.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA; Companies Act 2013; SAs issued by ICAI; Income-tax Act 2025 (tax year 2026-27, Finance Act 2026); CGST/IGST Acts after the September 2025 rate rationalisation; Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016

lesson.heading: Revenue over time for EPC contracts
lesson.body:
Ind AS 115 recognises revenue over time if any one of these is met: the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits; the entity's work creates or enhances an asset the customer controls as it is created (a highway built on government land); or the asset has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for work done to date.

Progress is measured by an output or input method. The common input method is cost-to-cost:

| Step | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Progress | Cost incurred to date / total estimated cost |
| Cumulative revenue | Transaction price x progress |
| Revenue this year | Cumulative revenue - revenue recognised in earlier years |

Costs that do not reflect performance (uninstalled materials, wasted material, unexpected rework) are excluded from the progress measure.

**Onerous contracts**: when the unavoidable cost of a contract exceeds its consideration, the whole expected loss is recognised at once. The loss already embedded in revenue and cost to date is part of it; the balance is a provision under Ind AS 37.

lesson.heading: Project finance: DSCR and covenants
lesson.body:
Infrastructure SPVs borrow against project cash flows. Lenders test the debt service coverage ratio:

DSCR = cash flow available for debt service / (interest + principal due).

A DSCR below the covenant (often 1.20-1.30) is an event of default under the loan agreement.

Ind AS 1: if a covenant breach on or before the reporting date makes a long-term loan repayable on demand, the loan is classified as current, even if the lender agrees after the reporting date not to demand repayment. It stays non-current only if the lender gave, by the reporting date, a grace period of at least twelve months after the reporting date.

For the auditor, a breach is also an indicator for going concern (SA 570) and for impairment of the SPV investment (Ind AS 36).

lesson.heading: Real estate: RERA, GST and the stamp duty value rule
lesson.body:
**RERA** (section 4(2)(l)(D) of the RERA Act 2016): 70% of the amounts realised from allottees for a project are deposited in a separate bank account and used only for construction and land cost of that project. Withdrawals are in proportion to completion, certified by an engineer, an architect and a practising chartered accountant.

**GST on residential flats** (rates notified under the CGST Act; verify before the exam):

| Supply | GST |
| --- | --- |
| Affordable residential apartment under construction | 1% effective, no ITC |
| Other residential apartment under construction | 5% effective (7.5% on value after a deemed one-third deduction for land), no ITC |
| Sale of a flat after the completion certificate | Not a supply (Schedule III: sale of building), no GST |

**Stamp duty value rule for the seller** (corresponds to section 43CA of the 1961 Act): if a builder transfers land or building held as stock for less than the stamp duty value, and the stamp duty value exceeds 110% of the consideration, the stamp duty value is taken as the full value of consideration. The buyer may be taxed on the difference (corresponds to section 56(2)(x)).

lesson.heading: Company law and audit points
lesson.body:
- **Section 186(11) and Schedule VI**: a company engaged in providing infrastructural facilities (roads, highways, ports, power, water supply and others listed in Schedule VI) is exempt from section 186 (except sub-section (1)) for loans, guarantees and securities. Infrastructure groups therefore lend to SPVs without the 60%/100% limit.
- **Ind AS 23**: a real estate project under development is a qualifying asset, so borrowing costs are included in inventory until the project is substantially ready.
- **Going concern (SA 570)**: stalled projects, RERA penalties, DSCR breaches and refund claims from allottees are classic indicators. The auditor evaluates management's plans (asset sales, funding from special situation funds) and modifies the report or adds a material uncertainty paragraph as needed.
- **Accounting estimates (SA 540)**: total estimated cost to complete drives revenue; test the budget, change orders and site progress reports.

lesson.heading: Strategy: asset-heavy vs asset-light
lesson.body:
Real estate developers that buy land outright lock up capital. The asset-light alternative is a joint development agreement (JDA): the landowner contributes land and receives a share of flats or revenue; the developer contributes construction and brand. This improves return on capital employed but brings tax (capital gains for the landowner on the JDA) and GST questions.

In infrastructure, the hybrid annuity model (HAM) shares risk: the authority pays part of the project cost during construction and annuities later, so the developer carries less traffic risk than in a BOT toll project.

A strategy answer compares risk, capital need and return for each model and links it to the case's balance sheet (debt level, DSCR).

keyPoints: Over time if the customer controls the asset as it is built; progress = cost to date / total estimated cost.
Onerous contract: recognise the full expected loss at once; balance beyond loss to date is an Ind AS 37 provision.
DSCR = CFADS / (interest + principal); covenant breach at the reporting date makes the loan current under Ind AS 1.
RERA: 70% of collections into a separate account; withdrawals certified by engineer, architect and CA.
GST: 1% affordable, 5% other under-construction flats, no ITC; no GST after completion certificate.
Stamp duty value rule: if SDV exceeds 110% of consideration, SDV is the consideration (corresponds to section 43CA).
Section 186(11): infrastructure companies are exempt from section 186 except sub-section (1).

cases.title: Case: Meridian Infra and Realty Ltd - EPC and toll SPV
cases.body:
Meridian Infra and Realty Ltd (MIRL) is a listed Ind AS company in Hyderabad with two segments: EPC contracts for roads and metro works, and residential real estate. It owns 100% of Meridian Tollways Pvt Ltd (MTPL), a BOT toll road SPV.

**EPC contracts at 31 March 2027 (₹ crore)**

| Contract | Price | Total estimated cost | Cost incurred to date | Revenue recognised earlier |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| State highway (government land) | 500 | 400 | 140 | Nil (started this year) |
| Metro depot | 300 | 330 (revised in March 2027) | 132 | Nil (started this year) |

The metro depot estimate rose from ₹270 crore to ₹330 crore after a design change that the client has refused to pay for.

**MTPL, FY 2026-27 (₹ crore)**: cash flow available for debt service 90; interest due 40; principal due 30. The loan agreement requires a minimum DSCR of 1.30; a breach makes the loan repayable on demand. The lender's waiver letter was received on 20 April 2027, after the year end.

cases.title: Case: Meridian Infra and Realty Ltd - Meridian Heights project
cases.body:
Meridian Heights is a residential project in Pune registered under RERA. It is not an affordable housing project. Facts for FY 2026-27:

- Amounts realised from allottees during the year: ₹400 crore.
- An under-construction flat was booked for ₹1.20 crore (excluding GST), including the land share; no separate land value is charged.
- In Tower A the completion certificate was received in October 2026; 12 flats were sold after that date.
- One unsold flat (held as stock-in-trade) was sold in February 2027 for ₹2.00 crore; its stamp duty value on the date of the agreement was ₹2.25 crore. No part of the consideration was received before the agreement date.
- MIRL gave a corporate guarantee of ₹500 crore for MTPL's loan. MIRL's paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium total ₹800 crore.
- Two older projects in Nagpur have stalled for 18 months; 140 allottees have filed refund claims before the RERA authority.

questions.prompt: Compute the revenue MIRL recognises in FY 2026-27 on the state highway contract. Answer in ₹ crore.
questions.explanation:
The highway is built on government land, so the customer controls the asset as it is created: revenue over time.

| Step | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Progress = 140 / 400 | 35% |
| Revenue = 500 x 35% | **175** |
| Cost | 140 |
| Margin | 35 |

questions.prompt: Compute the total loss MIRL recognises in FY 2026-27 on the metro depot contract (loss on work done plus any onerous contract provision). Answer in ₹ crore.
questions.explanation:
| Step | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Progress = 132 / 330 | 40% |
| Revenue = 300 x 40% | 120 |
| Cost to date | (132) |
| Loss on work done | (12) |
| Provision for remaining loss: total loss (330 - 300) 30 - 12 | (18) |
| **Total loss recognised** | **(30)** |

The whole expected loss of ₹30 crore is recognised at once; the ₹18 crore balance is an onerous contract provision under Ind AS 37.

questions.prompt: Compute MTPL's DSCR for FY 2026-27. Answer in times to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: DSCR = 90 / (40 + 30) = **1.29 times**, below the 1.30 covenant.

questions.prompt: How should MTPL classify its term loan at 31 March 2027?
options: Current, because the covenant was breached at the reporting date and the waiver came after the year end
Non-current, because the waiver was received before the financial statements were approved
Non-current, because the breach is small
Split equally between current and non-current
questions.explanation: Under Ind AS 1, a breach on or before the reporting date that makes the loan payable on demand requires current classification unless, by the reporting date, the lender agreed to a grace period of at least twelve months. A waiver received on 20 April 2027 is a non-adjusting event; disclose it.

questions.prompt: Which Ind AS 115 criterion supports recognising revenue over time on the state highway contract?
options: MIRL's work creates an asset that the customer controls as it is created
The customer pays a mobilisation advance
The contract is longer than one year
MIRL has a fixed price contract
questions.explanation: The highway is on government land, so the government controls the work in progress as it is built. An advance, contract length or price type does not by itself determine over-time recognition.

questions.prompt: How much of the year's collections must MIRL deposit in the Meridian Heights RERA separate account? Answer in ₹ crore.
questions.explanation: RERA requires 70% of amounts realised from allottees to be kept in a separate account: 400 x 70% = **₹280 crore**. Withdrawals must be in proportion to completion, certified by an engineer, an architect and a practising CA.

questions.prompt: Compute the GST payable on the under-construction flat booked for ₹1.20 crore. Answer in ₹ lakh to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
Value of construction service = total amount less deemed land value of one-third = 120 x 2/3 = ₹80 lakh.

GST at 7.5% (CGST 3.75% + SGST 3.75%) = 80 x 7.5% = **₹6.00 lakh**, an effective 5% of ₹120 lakh. No ITC is available at this rate.

questions.prompt: What is the full value of consideration for computing MIRL's business income on the unsold flat? Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: SDV / consideration = 2.25 / 2.00 = 112.5%, above the 110% tolerance. Under the stamp duty value rule for stock-in-trade (corresponds to section 43CA of the 1961 Act), the SDV of **₹2.25 crore** is the full value of consideration. Had the SDV been ₹2.18 crore (109%), the actual ₹2.00 crore would apply.

questions.prompt: Does MIRL's ₹500 crore guarantee for MTPL's loan need a special resolution under section 186?
options: No: MIRL provides infrastructural facilities, so section 186(11) exempts the guarantee from section 186 except sub-section (1)
Yes: ₹500 crore exceeds 60% of ₹800 crore
Yes: all guarantees above ₹100 crore need a special resolution
No: guarantees are never covered by section 186
questions.explanation: Roads are infrastructural facilities under Schedule VI. Section 186(11) exempts loans, guarantees and securities given by such companies from section 186 except sub-section (1) (two layers of investment companies). The guarantee is also exempt from special resolution because MTPL is wholly owned. Section 188 and Ind AS 24 disclosures still apply.

questions.prompt: What is the GST position on the 12 Tower A flats sold after the completion certificate?
options: No GST: sale of a building after the completion certificate is neither a supply of goods nor services
GST at 5% without ITC
GST at 1% as they are completed
GST at 18% with ITC
questions.explanation: Schedule III of the CGST Act treats sale of land and, subject to the construction exception, sale of a building as neither goods nor services. Once the completion certificate is issued, the sale of a flat attracts stamp duty, not GST. MIRL must reverse common ITC attributable to these exempt supplies.

questions.prompt: An onerous contract loss is recognised gradually as the contract progresses, in line with the percentage of completion.
questions.explanation: When total estimated cost exceeds the contract price, the entire expected loss is recognised immediately: the part embedded in work done plus a provision for the rest under Ind AS 37.

questions.prompt: Under Ind AS 115, which of these conditions lead to revenue being recognised over time? Select all that apply.
options: The customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits as the entity performs
The entity's performance creates or enhances an asset the customer controls as it is created
The asset has no alternative use to the entity and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date
The customer has paid more than 50% of the price in advance
The contract runs for more than twelve months
questions.explanation: Paragraph 35 of Ind AS 115 lists three criteria; meeting any one gives over-time recognition. Advances and contract duration are not criteria.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under the RERA Act 2016, ___ percent of the amounts realised from allottees must be deposited in a separate account for the project.
questions.explanation: Section 4(2)(l)(D) of the RERA Act requires 70% of amounts realised for the project from allottees to be deposited in a separate account in a scheduled bank.

questions.prompt: Prepare the extract of MIRL's statement of profit and loss for the two EPC contracts and the journal entry for the onerous contract provision.
questions.data: State highway: price ₹500 crore, total estimated cost ₹400 crore, cost incurred ₹140 crore. Metro depot: price ₹300 crore, total estimated cost ₹330 crore, cost incurred ₹132 crore. Both started in FY 2026-27.

**Extract, FY 2026-27 (₹ crore)**

| Particulars | Highway | Metro depot | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Revenue from contracts | 175 | 120 | 295 |
| Contract costs | (140) | (132) | (272) |
| Onerous contract provision | - | (18) | (18) |
| **Contract result** | **35** | **(30)** | **5** |

**Journal entry**

| --- | --- | --- |

| To Provision for onerous contract (Ind AS 37) | | 18 |

Disclose the change in estimate (Ind AS 8) and the disputed design change claim as a contingent asset only if inflow is probable.

questions.prompt: As auditor of MIRL, how would you evaluate going concern given the stalled Nagpur projects and MTPL's covenant breach?
questions.answer:
- Identify events and conditions (SA 570): stalled projects for 18 months, 140 refund claims before RERA, DSCR of 1.29 against 1.30 with the loan current at year end, and the ₹500 crore guarantee that could crystallise.
- Obtain management's assessment for at least twelve months from the reporting date and its cash flow forecast; test assumptions on collections, asset sales and fresh funding.
- Read the lender's waiver (20 April 2027) as subsequent evidence (SA 560) and check its conditions.
- Evaluate provisions for refunds and interest to allottees (Ind AS 37) and whether the guarantee needs recognition under Ind AS 109.
- Conclude: if a material uncertainty exists and is adequately disclosed, add a "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" section (SA 570, SA 706 style); if disclosure is inadequate, qualify or give an adverse opinion (SA 705).

questions.prompt: Should MIRL move its real estate segment to an asset-light joint development model? Discuss.
questions.answer:
- Today MIRL buys land outright, so capital is locked in land for years and debt is high (MTPL already breaches its DSCR).
- Under a JDA the landowner contributes land for a share of flats or revenue. MIRL's capital need falls sharply, ROCE improves and project starts are faster.
- Costs: lower margin per project (land share given away), dependence on landowner disputes, and tax and GST complexity (the landowner's capital gains on the JDA, GST on development rights and on flats given to the landowner).
- Strategic fit: MIRL's strengths are construction and brand, not land banking; the JDA lets it play to them (resource-based view).
- Recommendation: use JDAs for new launches in Pune, keep RERA compliance tight to protect the brand, and use released capital to reduce debt.
