chapters.title: Case Set: IT Services and a Startup
chapters.summary: A SaaS startup raising venture capital: Ind AS 115 for software bundles, Ind AS 102 ESOPs, the VC valuation method, export of services under GST, ESOP perquisite tax, startup company law relaxations, SA 402 and scale-up strategy.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA; Companies Act 2013; SAs issued by ICAI; Income-tax Act 2025 (tax year 2026-27, Finance Act 2026); CGST/IGST Acts after the September 2025 rate rationalisation

lesson.heading: Revenue from software bundles (Ind AS 115)
lesson.body:
Software contracts bundle a licence, implementation and support. Apply the five steps: identify the contract, identify distinct performance obligations, determine the price, allocate it on relative standalone selling prices (SSP), and recognise revenue as each obligation is satisfied.

| Obligation | Typical timing |
| --- | --- |
| Term licence to use software as it exists (right to use) | Point in time, when the customer can use it |
| SaaS subscription (right to access hosted software) | Over time, straight-line over the term |
| Implementation that does not significantly customise the software | Separate obligation, over time as performed |
| Post-contract support and updates | Over time, over the support period |

If implementation significantly modifies the software, licence and implementation are not distinct and form one obligation.

Worked allocation: price ₹60 lakh; SSPs ₹40 lakh, ₹15 lakh and ₹25 lakh (total ₹80 lakh). Allocation = 60 x SSP / 80, giving ₹30 lakh, ₹11.25 lakh and ₹18.75 lakh.

lesson.heading: ESOPs: accounting, tax and company law
lesson.body:
**Ind AS 102 (equity-settled)**: measure options at grant-date fair value; recognise the expense over the vesting period, based on the best estimate of options expected to vest, with a true-up each year. Market conditions are not trued up; service and non-market conditions are.

| Year | Cumulative expense |
| --- | --- |
| Year n | Options expected to vest x fair value x n / vesting years |
| Expense for the year | Cumulative to date - cumulative to last year |

**Tax in the employee's hands**: on allotment, the perquisite is the fair market value on the date of exercise less the amount paid. For employees of an eligible startup the tax on this perquisite is deferred to the earliest of the end of the deferral window (48 months), sale of the shares, or leaving the employer.

**Companies Act**: ESOPs cannot normally be granted to promoters or to directors holding more than 10% of equity, but a DPIIT-recognised startup may grant them to such persons for up to ten years from incorporation (Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules).

lesson.heading: Valuing a startup: the VC method
lesson.body:
Early-stage companies have losses, so DCF is unreliable. The venture capital method works back from an exit:

- Exit value = expected metric in exit year x exit multiple (for SaaS, often EV / revenue).
- Post-money value today = exit value / (1 + target return)^years.
- Required stake = investment / post-money value. Pre-money = post-money - investment.
- If later rounds will dilute the investor, required stake today = stake at exit / retention ratio.

Target returns of 30-50% reflect the high failure rate. Discuss sensitivity: a lower multiple or a delayed exit cuts the post-money value sharply.

lesson.heading: GST and tax on cross-border IT services
lesson.body:
**Export of services** (section 2(6) of the IGST Act) requires: supplier in India, recipient outside India, place of supply outside India, payment received in convertible foreign exchange (or in INR where RBI permits), and the supplier and recipient not being merely establishments of the same person. Exports are zero-rated (section 16 of the IGST Act): supply under LUT without tax and claim refund of unused ITC, or pay IGST and claim refund.

**Angel tax**: the old rule taxing share premium above fair value received by a closely held company (section 56(2)(viib) of the 1961 Act) was omitted from tax year 2024-25 (AY 2025-26). It is not carried into the Income-tax Act 2025, so a premium round is not taxed in the startup's hands on that ground.

**Audit**: when a startup uses a cloud provider for billing or payroll, the auditor of the startup (user auditor) applies SA 402 and relies on a Type 2 service organisation report (design and operating effectiveness of controls) plus complementary user entity controls.

lesson.heading: Strategy for scaling a SaaS business
lesson.body:
- **Unit economics**: customer acquisition cost (CAC), lifetime value (LTV), net revenue retention and churn decide whether growth creates value. An LTV/CAC ratio of 3 or more is a common benchmark.
- **Network effects and switching costs** create defensibility (Porter: they raise entry barriers).
- **Blue ocean**: target a niche (for example, compliance software for mid-sized hospitals) where rivals are absent, instead of fighting large incumbents.
- **Balanced scorecard**: financial (ARR, burn rate), customer (churn, NPS), internal process (uptime, deployment speed), learning and growth (engineering attrition, ESOP coverage).

Common mistake: recommending aggressive growth when the case shows the runway (cash / monthly burn) is under 12 months.

keyPoints: Allocate the bundle price on relative SSP; licence at a point in time, support over time.
Ind AS 102: grant-date fair value x options expected to vest, spread over vesting, trued up for service conditions.
ESOP perquisite = FMV on exercise date - exercise price; deferred for eligible startup employees.
VC method: post-money = exit value / (1 + target return)^n; stake = investment / post-money.
Export of services: five conditions of section 2(6) IGST Act; zero-rated under LUT or with refund.
Angel tax (section 56(2)(viib) of the 1961 Act) omitted from AY 2025-26.
Startups may grant ESOPs to promoters for ten years from incorporation; SA 402 for cloud service providers.

cases.title: Case: CodeNest Technologies Pvt Ltd - contracts, ESOPs and funding
cases.body:
CodeNest Technologies Pvt Ltd (CNT), Bengaluru, was incorporated in 2021 and is recognised by DPIIT as a startup. It sells hospital management software to clinics in India and the USA and follows Ind AS (it is a subsidiary of a listed investor). Year end 31 March.

**Contract with Medilink Hospitals (signed 1 October 2026), total price ₹60 lakh**

| Element | Standalone selling price (₹ lakh) | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Three-year term licence (software as it exists; no significant customisation) | 40 | Delivered 1 October 2026 |
| Implementation and data migration | 15 | Completed 31 December 2026 |
| Support and updates for one year | 25 | 1 October 2026 to 30 September 2027 |

**ESOPs**: on 1 April 2026 CNT granted 1,000 options each to 50 employees, vesting after three years of service. Grant-date fair value ₹300 per option. At 31 March 2027 CNT expects 10% of the options to lapse because of attrition.

**Series B**: a VC fund will invest ₹25 crore. It expects CNT's revenue in Year 5 to be ₹200 crore and an exit at 6 times revenue, and targets a 40% annual return.

cases.title: Case: CodeNest Technologies Pvt Ltd - tax, law and audit
cases.body:
Further facts for FY 2026-27:

- CNT provides software support to Carewell Inc, an unrelated US hospital group, from Bengaluru, invoiced in USD and paid into CNT's bank account in USD. CNT has furnished an LUT.
- In Series A (2023) CNT issued shares at a premium; the founders ask whether the Series B premium can be taxed in CNT's hands.
- Riya, an employee, exercised 2,000 vested options from an earlier plan at ₹100 per share in January 2027, when the FMV was ₹800 per share.
- The founders (holding 35% each) want ESOPs for themselves.
- CNT's billing, revenue records and payroll run on a third-party cloud ERP. The statutory auditor plans to rely on the ERP provider's controls.

questions.prompt: Compute the revenue CNT recognises in FY 2026-27 from the Medilink contract. Answer in ₹ lakh to 3 decimals.
questions.explanation:
| Obligation | Allocation (60 x SSP / 80) | Recognised in FY 2026-27 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Term licence (point in time, 1 Oct 2026) | 30.00 | 30.000 |
| Implementation (done by 31 Dec 2026) | 11.25 | 11.250 |
| Support (6 of 12 months) | 18.75 | 9.375 |
| **Total** | **60.00** | **50.625** |

The balance ₹9.375 lakh is a contract liability (deferred revenue) at year end.

questions.prompt: Compute CNT's ESOP expense for FY 2026-27 under Ind AS 102. Answer in ₹ lakh.
questions.explanation:
Options expected to vest = 50 x 1,000 x 90% = 45,000.

Expense for Year 1 = 45,000 x ₹300 x 1/3 = **₹45 lakh** (Dr Employee benefits expense, Cr Share-based payment reserve).

questions.prompt: Using the VC method, compute the stake the fund should ask for in exchange for ₹25 crore. Answer as a % to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
- Exit value = 200 x 6 = ₹1,200 crore.
- Post-money value today = 1,200 / 1.4^5 = 1,200 / 5.37824 = ₹223.12 crore.
- Required stake = 25 / 223.12 = **11.20%**.
- Pre-money value = 223.12 - 25 = ₹198.12 crore.

questions.prompt: Why is the implementation service a separate performance obligation in the Medilink contract?
options: It does not significantly modify the software, so the customer can benefit from the licence and the service separately
It is invoiced separately
It is performed by a different team
It has a lower margin than the licence
questions.explanation: A good or service is distinct if the customer can benefit from it on its own or with readily available resources, and it is separately identifiable in the contract. Implementation without significant customisation meets both tests. Invoicing, team or margin do not decide distinctness.

questions.prompt: If the fund expects its stake to be diluted by a later round in which existing holders retain 80% of their holding, what stake should it ask for now?
options: About 14.01%
About 8.96%
About 11.20%, as dilution does not matter
About 50%
questions.explanation: Required stake at exit is 11.20%. With a retention ratio of 0.8, the stake today must be 11.20 / 0.8 = 14.01% so that after dilution the fund still holds the stake it needs.

questions.prompt: What is the GST position of CNT's support services to Carewell Inc?
options: Export of services, zero-rated; CNT supplies under LUT without IGST and may claim refund of unused ITC
Taxable at 18% IGST as CNT is located in India
Exempt supply, so ITC must be reversed
Not a supply because the recipient is outside India
questions.explanation: Supplier in India, recipient outside India, place of supply (location of recipient) outside India, payment in convertible foreign exchange, and the parties are unrelated: all section 2(6) conditions are met. Exports are zero-rated under section 16 of the IGST Act, not exempt, so ITC is not reversed.

questions.prompt: Can the Series B share premium be taxed in CNT's hands as income because it exceeds fair market value?
options: No: the angel tax provision (section 56(2)(viib) of the 1961 Act) was omitted from AY 2025-26
Yes: premium above FMV is always income of a closely held company
Yes, unless the investor is a foreign fund
Only the premium above ₹25 crore is taxable
questions.explanation: The Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 omitted section 56(2)(viib) from AY 2025-26 (tax year 2024-25 onward), and the Income-tax Act 2025 does not reintroduce it. Share premium is a capital receipt for CNT; FEMA pricing rules still apply to foreign investors.

questions.prompt: Compute the perquisite value taxable in Riya's hands on the exercise of options. Answer in ₹ lakh.
questions.explanation: Perquisite = (FMV on exercise date - exercise price) x shares = (800 - 100) x 2,000 = ₹14,00,000 = **₹14 lakh**. As CNT is an eligible startup, tax on it may be deferred to the earliest of the end of the 48-month window, sale of the shares or Riya leaving CNT. Her cost for capital gains is the FMV of ₹800 per share.

questions.prompt: Can CNT grant ESOPs to the founders, who hold 35% each?
options: Yes, because CNT is a DPIIT-recognised startup within ten years of incorporation
No, promoters can never receive ESOPs
Yes, but only if CNT is listed
Yes, with Central Government approval only
questions.explanation: The Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules bar ESOPs to promoters and to directors holding more than 10% of equity, but relax this for a startup up to ten years from incorporation. CNT was incorporated in 2021, so it qualifies until 2031 if it stays a recognised startup.

questions.prompt: Under Ind AS 102, a company re-estimates the number of options expected to vest each year for employees leaving before vesting, and adjusts the cumulative expense.
questions.explanation: Service conditions are non-market vesting conditions. The entity revises its estimate of options expected to vest at each reporting date and on vesting trues up to the actual number. The grant-date fair value is not remeasured.

questions.prompt: Which conditions must all be met for a supply of services to be an export of services under section 2(6) of the IGST Act?
options: The supplier is located in India
The recipient is located outside India
The place of supply is outside India
Payment is received in convertible foreign exchange or in INR where RBI permits
The supplier has no domestic customers
questions.explanation: Section 2(6) also requires that supplier and recipient are not merely establishments of a distinct person. Having domestic customers does not affect export status.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: when a user entity relies on a cloud provider's controls, its auditor applies SA ___, Audit Considerations Relating to an Entity Using a Service Organisation.
questions.explanation: SA 402 covers the user auditor's work, including the use of Type 1 and Type 2 reports from the service auditor.

questions.prompt: Pass the Ind AS 102 journal entries for CNT's ESOP for all three years.
questions.data: 50,000 options granted on 1 April 2026; grant-date fair value ₹300; vesting after three years of service. Expected lapses: 10% at 31 March 2027, 15% at 31 March 2028. Actual options vested on 31 March 2029: 41,000.
questions.answer:
**Workings (₹ lakh)**

| Year end | Options expected or vested | Cumulative expense | Expense for the year |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 31 Mar 2027 | 45,000 | 45,000 x 300 x 1/3 = 45.00 | 45.00 |
| 31 Mar 2028 | 42,500 | 42,500 x 300 x 2/3 = 85.00 | 40.00 |
| 31 Mar 2029 | 41,000 | 41,000 x 300 = 123.00 | 38.00 |

**Journal entry each year**

| Entry | Dr | Cr |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Employee benefits expense Dr | 45.00 / 40.00 / 38.00 | |
| To Share-based payment reserve (equity) | | 45.00 / 40.00 / 38.00 |

On exercise: Dr Bank (exercise price) and Dr Share-based payment reserve; Cr Equity share capital and Cr Securities premium. Lapsed vested options: transfer the reserve to retained earnings (no reversal through profit or loss).

questions.prompt: CNT has 14 months of cash runway and plans to double its US sales team. Advise on strategy and funding.
questions.answer:
- Check unit economics first: if LTV/CAC is below 3 or churn is high, doubling sales spend burns cash without value.
- Raise the Series B (post-money about ₹223.12 crore at the fund's terms) before runway falls under 12 months, since negotiating power drops as cash runs down.
- Focus (Porter) or blue ocean: concentrate on the clinic segment where CNT already wins rather than chasing large hospital chains against incumbents.
- Protect the export model: keep LUT compliance and FEMA realisation timelines so GST refunds and cash flow are not delayed.
- Use a balanced scorecard: ARR growth and burn multiple (financial), churn and NPS (customer), uptime and release cadence (process), engineer attrition and ESOP coverage (learning).
- Recommendation: expand the US team in phases tied to pipeline milestones, funded by the Series B.

questions.prompt: Explain how the statutory auditor of CNT should use the cloud ERP provider's controls report.
questions.answer: Under SA 402 the auditor first understands the services, their significance to financial reporting (billing, revenue and payroll) and the controls at CNT that interact with the ERP. A Type 1 report covers only the design of controls at a point in time; to rely on operating effectiveness the auditor needs a Type 2 report covering a period that overlaps the audit year. The auditor evaluates the service auditor's competence and independence, the scope, exceptions noted and any carve-out of sub-service organisations, and tests the complementary user entity controls listed in the report (for example, user access reviews at CNT). Where the period does not cover the year, the auditor gets a bridge letter and performs additional procedures. The auditor's report does not refer to the service auditor's report (SA 402).

chapters.title: Case Set: FMCG and Retail
chapters.summary: A consumer products company selling through distributors and its own stores: variable consideration, returns, loyalty points, payments to retailers, working capital, CSR, GST on discounts and samples, royalty TDS, inventory audit and portfolio strategy.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA; Companies Act 2013; SAs issued by ICAI; Income-tax Act 2025 (tax year 2026-27, Finance Act 2026); CGST/IGST Acts after the September 2025 rate rationalisation

lesson.heading: Revenue in FMCG: variable consideration
lesson.body:
FMCG revenue is full of variable consideration: volume rebates, trade schemes, expected returns, cash discounts. Ind AS 115 requires the entity to estimate it (expected value or most likely amount) and include it only to the extent a significant reversal is highly unlikely.

| Item | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Expected returns | Reduce revenue; recognise a refund liability; recognise an asset (right to recover goods) at former carrying amount less recovery costs, and reduce cost of sales |
| Volume rebates and trade schemes | Reduce revenue; refund liability to the distributor |
| Loyalty points | Separate performance obligation (material right); allocate price on relative SSP, defer revenue until points are redeemed or expire |
| Slotting or listing fees paid to retailers | Consideration payable to a customer: reduce revenue unless in exchange for a distinct good or service at fair value |
| Free samples to consumers | Marketing expense, not revenue |

Worked example: retail sales ₹100 crore with points whose SSP is ₹5 crore. Allocation to points = 100 x 5 / 105 = ₹4.76 crore, deferred.

lesson.heading: Working capital and value metrics
lesson.body:
FMCG companies often run on negative or very low working capital because distributors pay quickly and suppliers give credit.

- Inventory days = inventory / cost of goods sold x 365.
- Receivable days = trade receivables / revenue x 365.
- Payable days = trade payables / purchases x 365.
- Cash conversion cycle (CCC) = inventory days + receivable days - payable days.

EVA = NOPAT - WACC x capital employed. A brand-heavy business has high EVA because its capital base is small. In the exam, compute the metric and then interpret it: a short CCC funds growth internally; stretching payables too far risks supplier relations and MSME payment rules (45-day limit under the MSMED Act and the related tax disallowance).

lesson.heading: GST: discounts, schemes and samples
lesson.body:
- **Discounts before or at supply** shown on the invoice reduce the taxable value (section 15(3)(a) of the CGST Act).
- **Post-supply discounts** reduce value only if agreed before or at supply, linked to specific invoices, and the recipient reverses the related ITC (section 15(3)(b)); the supplier issues a tax credit note under section 34. Otherwise, issue a financial credit note without reducing GST.
- **Free samples and gifts**: ITC on goods given as free samples or gifts is blocked (section 17(5)(h)); so is ITC on goods lost, stolen, destroyed or written off. Gifts to employees up to ₹50,000 a year are not a supply.
- **Buy one get one free** is one supply of two items at one price, not a free supply; ITC is available on both.

**Royalty to a foreign brand owner**: tax is deducted at the rate in the Act or, if lower, the DTAA rate when the payee furnishes a tax residency certificate and the prescribed details (the treaty override corresponds to section 90(2) of the 1961 Act). The payment also falls under transfer pricing if the payee is an associated enterprise.

lesson.heading: Audit and company law in FMCG
lesson.body:
- **Revenue cut-off** at year end (dispatches to distributors in the last week, stock pushed into the channel) is a fraud risk: SA 240 presumes a risk of fraud in revenue recognition.
- **Inventory at depots and stores**: attend counts (SA 501), test expiry and NRV. CARO 2020 clause 3(ii)(a) asks whether discrepancies of 10% or more in aggregate for each class of inventory were noticed on physical verification and properly dealt with.
- **CSR (section 135)**: applies if, in the immediately preceding financial year, net worth is ₹500 crore or more, or turnover ₹1,000 crore or more, or net profit ₹5 crore or more. Spend at least 2% of average net profits (computed under section 198) of the three immediately preceding financial years. Unspent amounts go to a Schedule VII fund within six months, or to an Unspent CSR Account for ongoing projects.

lesson.heading: Strategy: brands and portfolios
lesson.body:
- **BCG matrix**: a leading brand in a mature category is a cash cow (high share, low growth); a new health-food brand with small share in a fast-growing category is a question mark. Cash cows fund question marks; dogs are harvested or divested.
- **Generic strategies**: mass brands compete on cost leadership (distribution reach, scale purchasing); premium brands on differentiation.
- **Distribution**: modern trade and quick commerce grow faster than general trade but demand higher margins and listing fees. Direct-to-consumer channels give data but cost more per order.

Answer pattern: classify the case's brands, show the cash flows between them, and recommend where to invest, citing the case figures.

keyPoints: Expected returns and rebates reduce revenue; refund liability plus an asset for goods expected back.
Loyalty points: allocate on relative SSP and defer until redemption.
Payments to retailers reduce revenue unless for a distinct good or service.
CCC = inventory days + receivable days - payable days.
Section 15(3)(b): post-supply discount reduces value only if pre-agreed, invoice-linked and ITC reversed.
Section 17(5)(h): no ITC on free samples, gifts, or goods destroyed or written off.
CSR: 2% of average net profits of the three preceding years; CARO 3(ii)(a): 10% inventory discrepancy test.

cases.title: Case: Annapurna Consumer Products Ltd - revenue and working capital
cases.body:
Annapurna Consumer Products Ltd (ACPL), Indore, is a listed Ind AS company selling packaged staples (atta, spices) and a new millet snack brand. It sells through 900 distributors and runs 120 own retail stores. Its brand is licensed from its Singapore parent.

**FY 2026-27 data (₹ crore)**

| Item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Invoiced sales to distributors | 500 |
| Expected returns (based on history) | 2% of invoiced sales |
| Cost of goods as % of sales | 60% |
| Volume rebates expected to be earned by distributors | 3% of invoiced sales |
| Sales in own stores (loyalty points issued) | 100 |
| Standalone selling price of points issued | 5 |
| Listing fees paid to a supermarket chain (no distinct service) | 4 |

**Working capital at 31 March 2027 (₹ crore)**: inventory 75, trade receivables 25, trade payables 100. Cost of goods sold 600, purchases 610, revenue for ratio purposes 475.

**Portfolio**: the atta brand has 28% share in a category growing 3% a year; the millet snack has 2% share in a category growing 25% a year.

cases.title: Case: Annapurna Consumer Products Ltd - tax, CSR and audit
cases.body:
Further facts:

- Net profits of ACPL computed under section 198: FY 2023-24 ₹210 crore, FY 2024-25 ₹240 crore, FY 2025-26 ₹270 crore.
- ACPL pays a brand royalty of ₹20 crore for FY 2026-27 to its Singapore parent. The parent has a tax residency certificate; assume the DTAA rate on royalty is 10% and lower than the rate under the Act.
- ACPL announced a year-end scheme: a 4% discount to distributors on March 2027 purchases, decided on 25 April 2027 and paid by credit notes.
- Free sample packs (GST paid on inputs ₹0.60 crore) were distributed in a promotion.
- Physical verification at three depots showed shortages of 12% in the spice category; the auditor noted heavy dispatches in the last five days of March 2027.

questions.prompt: Compute the revenue ACPL recognises on distributor sales for FY 2026-27, before the listing fee adjustment. Answer in ₹ crore.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ crore |
| --- | --- |
| Invoiced sales | 500 |
| Less: expected returns 2% | (10) |
| Less: expected volume rebates 3% | (15) |
| **Revenue** | **475** |

Refund liabilities of ₹25 crore are recognised. An asset for goods expected to be returned of 10 x 60% = ₹6 crore is recognised and cost of sales reduced by the same amount.

questions.prompt: How much of the ₹100 crore store sales is deferred as a contract liability for loyalty points? Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: Allocate on relative SSP: points = 100 x 5 / (100 + 5) = **₹4.76 crore**, deferred until redemption or expiry. Goods = ₹95.24 crore, recognised at the point of sale.

questions.prompt: How should ACPL account for the ₹4 crore listing fee paid to the supermarket chain?
options: Reduce revenue, as it is consideration payable to a customer with no distinct service received
Advertising expense
Capitalise as an intangible asset
Prepaid expense amortised over three years
questions.explanation: The supermarket is ACPL's customer. Under Ind AS 115, consideration payable to a customer reduces the transaction price unless it pays for a distinct good or service at fair value. The case states no distinct service.

questions.prompt: Compute ACPL's cash conversion cycle using year-end balances and a 365-day year. Answer in days to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
| Metric | Working | Days |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inventory days | 75 / 600 x 365 | 45.63 |
| Receivable days | 25 / 475 x 365 | 19.21 |
| Payable days | 100 / 610 x 365 | (59.84) |
| **CCC** | | **5.00** |

A five-day cycle means suppliers fund almost all of ACPL's inventory and receivables.

questions.prompt: Using the BCG matrix, how should ACPL classify its two brands?
options: Atta: cash cow; millet snack: question mark
Atta: star; millet snack: dog
Atta: dog; millet snack: star
Both are stars
questions.explanation: Atta has high relative share (28%) in a low-growth category (3%): cash cow. The millet snack has low share (2%) in a high-growth category (25%): question mark. Cash from atta can fund the snack until it gains share or is dropped.

questions.prompt: Compute ACPL's minimum CSR spend for FY 2026-27. Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: Average net profit of the three immediately preceding years = (210 + 240 + 270) / 3 = ₹240 crore. CSR = 2% x 240 = **₹4.80 crore** (section 135(5)).

questions.prompt: Compute the tax ACPL must deduct on the ₹20 crore royalty, applying the DTAA rate. Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: The payee may apply the DTAA where it is more beneficial (treaty override, corresponding to section 90(2) of the 1961 Act), given a tax residency certificate and the prescribed details. TDS = 20 x 10% = **₹2.00 crore**. No surcharge or cess is added to a treaty rate. The royalty is also an international transaction with an associated enterprise, so it must be at arm's length.

questions.prompt: Can ACPL reduce the GST value of March 2027 sales by the 4% discount decided on 25 April 2027?
options: No: the discount was not agreed before or at the time of supply, so it does not reduce value under section 15(3)(b); a financial credit note without GST is issued
Yes: any discount given by credit note reduces value
Yes, if distributors agree in writing after the event
No GST effect either way because discounts are exempt
questions.explanation: Section 15(3)(b) requires the post-supply discount to be established in terms of an agreement entered into at or before the time of supply and linked to specific invoices, with the recipient reversing the related ITC. A discount decided after the supply fails the first condition.

questions.prompt: What should the auditor report under CARO 2020 about the spice shortages?
options: Whether discrepancies of 10% or more in aggregate for the class were noticed and whether they were properly dealt with in the books (clause 3(ii)(a))
Nothing, as CARO does not cover inventory
Only shortages above 20% are reportable
Report the shortage to the Central Government as fraud
questions.explanation: A 12% shortage in a class of inventory crosses the 10% aggregate threshold in clause 3(ii)(a). The auditor states whether it was properly dealt with. Fraud reporting under section 143(12) arises only if the auditor has reason to believe a fraud has occurred.

questions.prompt: ACPL can take input tax credit of the ₹0.60 crore GST paid on inputs used for free sample packs.
questions.explanation: Section 17(5)(h) of the CGST Act blocks ITC on goods disposed of by way of gift or free samples. The ₹0.60 crore is a cost of the promotion.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduce ACPL's revenue under Ind AS 115?
options: Expected volume rebates to distributors
Expected sales returns
Listing fees paid to a retailer for no distinct service
Cost of free sample packs given to consumers
Freight on outward deliveries
questions.explanation: Rebates and returns are variable consideration; listing fees are consideration payable to a customer. Free samples are a marketing expense and outward freight is a selling or fulfilment cost.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: SA ___ requires the auditor to presume that there are risks of fraud in revenue recognition.
questions.explanation: SA 240 sets a rebuttable presumption of fraud risk in revenue recognition, which drives cut-off testing at year end.

questions.prompt: Pass the journal entries for ACPL's distributor sales with expected returns and rebates for FY 2026-27.
questions.data: Invoiced sales ₹500 crore (cash received or receivable); expected returns 2%; cost of goods 60% of sales; expected volume rebates 3%. Ignore GST.
questions.answer:
**Journal entries (₹ crore)**

| Entry | Dr | Cr |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trade receivables / Bank Dr | 500 | |
| To Revenue from operations | | 475 |
| To Refund liability - returns | | 10 |
| To Refund liability - volume rebates | | 15 |
| Cost of goods sold Dr | 294 | |
| Right to recover returned goods (asset) Dr | 6 | |
| To Inventory | | 300 |

Workings: returns 500 x 2% = 10; rebates 500 x 3% = 15; inventory issued 500 x 60% = 300; asset for goods expected back 10 x 60% = 6.

At each reporting date update the estimates; any change adjusts revenue (and the asset and cost of sales).

questions.prompt: The auditor notes heavy dispatches to distributors in the last five days of March 2027. What procedures should the auditor perform?
questions.answer:
- Treat it as a fraud risk in revenue recognition (SA 240) and a possible channel-stuffing scheme to meet targets.
- Test cut-off: match the last week's invoices with delivery proofs and transfer of control terms; goods in transit at year end are revenue only if control passed.
- Examine April 2027 credit notes and returns (SA 560): a spike indicates revenue that should not have been recognised.
- Confirm balances and scheme terms with selected distributors (SA 505); compare distributor stock levels with normal days of stock.
- Review management's estimate of returns and rebates (SA 540), and the related schemes announced after year end.
- Communicate findings to those charged with governance (SA 260) and consider the effect on the opinion (SA 705) if material misstatement remains.

questions.prompt: Recommend a portfolio strategy for ACPL's atta and millet snack brands.
questions.answer:
- Atta is a cash cow (28% share, 3% growth): defend share with cost leadership in sourcing and distribution, keep investment to maintenance, and harvest cash.
- The millet snack is a question mark (2% share, 25% growth): it needs heavy investment to become a star or should be dropped. Test it in modern trade and quick commerce where health snacks grow fastest; set a share target (say 6-8% in two years).
- Fund the snack from atta cash flows, keeping ACPL's short cash cycle (about five days).
- Watch costs that reduce revenue (listing fees, rebates) and track brand-level contribution, not just sales.
- Exit trigger: if the snack does not reach the share target, divest or reposition it, so cash is not trapped in a future dog.

chapters.title: Case Set: Pharma and Healthcare
chapters.summary: An export-oriented pharma company with a hospital arm: Ind AS 38 development costs, Ind AS 36 impairment after a USFDA warning letter, export receivable hedging, transfer pricing, material related party transactions, R&D tax deductions, healthcare GST and use of experts.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA; Companies Act 2013; SAs issued by ICAI; Income-tax Act 2025 (tax year 2026-27, Finance Act 2026); CGST/IGST Acts after the September 2025 rate rationalisation; SEBI LODR Regulations

lesson.heading: R&D and intangibles (Ind AS 38)
lesson.body:
Research costs are always expensed. Development costs are capitalised only from the date all six criteria are demonstrated: technical feasibility, intention to complete, ability to use or sell, how the asset will generate probable future economic benefits, availability of resources to complete, and reliable measurement of cost. Costs expensed earlier are not reinstated.

In pharma, the criteria are usually met late, often at regulatory filing or approval, because of the risk of failure in trials. In-process R&D acquired in a business combination is recognised separately at fair value under Ind AS 103, even though internal R&D of the same kind would be expensed.

| Cost | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Research (molecule screening) | Expense |
| Development before all criteria met | Expense |
| Development after all criteria met | Capitalise; amortise from availability for use |
| Intangible not yet available for use | Test for impairment annually |

lesson.heading: Impairment after a regulatory action (Ind AS 36)
lesson.body:
A USFDA warning letter or import alert on a plant is an impairment indicator for the cash-generating unit (CGU) that serves the US market.

- Recoverable amount = higher of fair value less costs of disposal (FVLCD) and value in use (VIU).
- Impairment loss = carrying amount - recoverable amount.
- Allocate the loss first to goodwill of the CGU, then to other assets pro rata to carrying amounts, without reducing any asset below the highest of its FVLCD, VIU and zero.

The same event drives other answers in a multidisciplinary case: inventory NRV (Ind AS 2) for stock that cannot be shipped, provisions or contingent liabilities (Ind AS 37) for remediation and customer claims, disclosure of a key audit matter (SA 701), consideration of non-compliance with laws and regulations (SA 250) and going concern (SA 570) if the US market is most of revenue.

lesson.heading: Hedging export receivables
lesson.body:
An exporter with USD receivables fears rupee appreciation.

| Method | Steps |
| --- | --- |
| Forward cover | Sell USD forward: rupees = USD x forward rate |
| Money market hedge | Borrow USD today equal to PV of the receivable, convert at spot, invest rupees till the due date; the receivable repays the USD loan |
| Option | Buy a USD put: protects downside, keeps upside, costs a premium |

Money market hedge: USD borrowed = receivable / (1 + USD rate x t); rupees at maturity = USD borrowed x spot x (1 + INR rate x t). Choose the method that gives the higher rupee inflow. Under Ind AS 109 the exporter can designate the forward as a cash flow hedge of a highly probable forecast sale.

lesson.heading: Tax and law for pharma groups
lesson.body:
- **Transfer pricing**: sales of APIs or formulations to a foreign subsidiary are international transactions with an associated enterprise. The price must be at arm's length (comparable uncontrolled price method where similar third-party sales exist). An adjustment increases Indian income: (ALP - actual price) x quantity.
- **R&D deductions**: revenue expenditure on scientific research related to the business and capital expenditure on it (other than land) are deductible in full (correspond to sections 35(1)(i) and 35(1)(iv) of the 1961 Act). These remain available in the concessional regime; the weighted deductions and deductions for payments to research associations do not.
- **Material related party transactions (SEBI LODR regulation 23)**: a transaction is material if it exceeds ₹1,000 crore or 10% of the listed entity's annual consolidated turnover, whichever is lower. Material RPTs need prior audit committee approval and shareholders' approval (related parties do not vote). Transactions with a wholly owned subsidiary whose accounts are consolidated are exempt from shareholders' approval.
- **Healthcare GST**: health care services by a clinical establishment, an authorised medical practitioner or paramedics are exempt; check the current notification for exceptions such as high-tariff non-ICU rooms.

lesson.heading: Strategy and audit in pharma
lesson.body:
- **Ansoff**: entering complex generics or biosimilars is product development; selling existing generics in new regulated markets is market development.
- **Strategic alliances**: in-licensing molecules from biotech startups, contract manufacturing (CDMO) for global innovators; both reduce R&D risk.
- **Value chain**: R&D and regulatory compliance are the primary sources of competitive advantage in regulated markets; a quality failure destroys it.
- **Using experts (SA 620)**: valuations of acquired IPR&D, VIU models and litigation assessments need an auditor's expert; the auditor evaluates the expert's competence, objectivity and work, and retains sole responsibility for the opinion.

keyPoints: Ind AS 38: capitalise development only after all six criteria are met; no reinstatement of earlier expense.
Ind AS 36: loss = carrying amount - higher of FVLCD and VIU; goodwill first, then pro rata.
Money market hedge for a receivable: borrow PV in USD, convert at spot, invest in INR.
Transfer pricing adjustment = (ALP - actual price) x quantity.
LODR regulation 23: material RPT above lower of ₹1,000 crore or 10% of consolidated turnover.
R&D revenue and capital expenditure (other than land) deductible in full, also in the concessional regime.
SA 620 for experts; SA 250 for regulatory non-compliance; SA 701 KAM for impairment.

cases.title: Case: Sanjeevani Pharma Ltd - R&D, impairment and exports
cases.body:
Sanjeevani Pharma Ltd (SPL), Ahmedabad, is a listed Ind AS company making generic formulations. 55% of its revenue comes from the USA. It holds 80% of Sanjeevani Inc (USA); a US partner holds 20%.

**R&D in FY 2026-27 (₹ crore)**: research on new molecules 30. Development of a complex injectable: 45 spent evenly over the year; all six Ind AS 38 criteria were demonstrated on 1 October 2026, and ₹18 crore was spent from that date.

**USFDA action**: in February 2027 the USFDA issued a warning letter to SPL's Baroda plant, the only plant approved for the US. Data for the US formulations CGU at 31 March 2027 (₹ crore):

| Asset | Carrying amount |
| --- | --- |
| Goodwill | 25 |
| Plant and machinery | 150 |
| Product intangibles (ANDAs) | 75 |
| **Total** | **250** |

Value in use ₹210 crore; fair value less costs of disposal ₹200 crore. The FVLCD of each individual asset is below its share of the loss.

**Export receivable**: USD 20 million due from a US distributor in three months. Spot ₹86.80/USD, three-month forward ₹87.50/USD, USD borrowing rate 6% p.a., rupee deposit rate 7.5% p.a.

cases.title: Case: Sanjeevani Pharma Ltd - group transactions and hospitals
cases.body:
Further facts:

- SPL sold 50,000 kg of an API to Sanjeevani Inc at ₹400 per kg. SPL sells the same API under similar terms to an unrelated US buyer at ₹460 per kg.
- SPL's consolidated turnover for FY 2025-26 was ₹8,000 crore. Sales to Sanjeevani Inc in FY 2027-28 are expected to be ₹900 crore.
- SPL bought R&D lab equipment for ₹12 crore and land for a new lab for ₹20 crore. SPL is in the concessional tax regime.
- SPL's subsidiary Sanjeevani Hospitals Pvt Ltd runs two multi-speciality hospitals.
- The auditor plans to rely on a valuation firm's VIU model for the US CGU.

questions.prompt: Compute the total R&D expense SPL charges to profit or loss in FY 2026-27. Answer in ₹ crore.
questions.explanation:
| Cost | ₹ crore | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Research | 30 | Expense |
| Development before 1 October 2026 (45 - 18) | 27 | Expense |
| Development from 1 October 2026 | 18 | Capitalise (intangible under development) |
| **Charged to P&L** | **57** | |

The ₹27 crore expensed earlier is not reinstated.

questions.prompt: Compute the impairment loss allocated to plant and machinery in the US formulations CGU. Answer in ₹ crore.
Compute the rupee inflow at the end of three months under a money market hedge for the USD 20 million receivable. Answer in ₹ crore to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
- USD borrowed today = 20 / (1 + 6% x 3/12) = USD 19.7044 million.
- Converted at spot 86.80 = ₹171.0345 crore.
- Invested at 7.5% for 3 months: 171.0345 x 1.01875 = **₹174.24 crore**.

The receivable of USD 20 million repays the USD loan with interest. Forward cover gives 20 x 87.50 = ₹175.00 crore, so the forward is better by about ₹0.76 crore.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a direct consequence of the USFDA warning letter for SPL's FY 2026-27 financial statements and audit?
options: Reclassification of the Baroda plant as investment property
Impairment testing of the US formulations CGU under Ind AS 36
Review of NRV of US-bound inventory under Ind AS 2
Consideration of non-compliance with laws and regulations under SA 250
questions.explanation: The plant is still used in production, so it remains property, plant and equipment. The warning letter triggers an impairment test, an NRV review of stock that may not be shipped, SA 250 procedures, a likely key audit matter and possibly going concern considerations.

questions.prompt: SPL's board plans to supply its existing generics to Brazil and Mexico for the first time. In Ansoff's terms this is:
options: Market development
Product development
Market penetration
Unrelated diversification
questions.explanation: Existing products sold in new markets is market development. It also reduces SPL's dependence on the US, where 55% of revenue now sits behind one plant under a warning letter.

questions.prompt: Compute the transfer pricing adjustment on the API sales to Sanjeevani Inc, using the comparable uncontrolled price method. Answer in ₹ lakh.
questions.explanation: Arm's length price (CUP) = ₹460 per kg. Adjustment = (460 - 400) x 50,000 kg = ₹30,00,000 = **₹30 lakh**, added to SPL's total income. Differences in terms, volume or market between the controlled and uncontrolled sales would need adjustment before using the CUP.

questions.prompt: What approvals do the FY 2027-28 sales of ₹900 crore to Sanjeevani Inc need under SEBI LODR?
options: Prior audit committee approval and shareholders' approval, as ₹900 crore exceeds the materiality threshold of ₹800 crore and the subsidiary is not wholly owned
Board approval only, as the threshold is ₹1,000 crore
No approval, as transactions with subsidiaries are always exempt
Central Government approval
questions.explanation: Threshold = lower of ₹1,000 crore and 10% of ₹8,000 crore = ₹800 crore. ₹900 crore is a material RPT. The exemption from shareholders' approval covers transactions with wholly owned subsidiaries only; Sanjeevani Inc is 80% owned. Related parties cannot vote on the resolution.

questions.prompt: How much deduction can SPL claim for the capital expenditure on its new R&D lab in the concessional regime?
options: ₹12 crore: capital expenditure on scientific research is deductible in full, but land is excluded
₹32 crore: equipment and land
Nil: the concessional regime bars all R&D deductions
₹18 crore: 150% weighted deduction on equipment
questions.explanation: Capital expenditure on scientific research related to the business, other than on land, is deductible in full (corresponds to section 35(1)(iv) of the 1961 Act), and this deduction is not withdrawn in the concessional regime. Weighted deductions are not available in that regime.

questions.prompt: What is the GST position of inpatient treatment provided by Sanjeevani Hospitals?
options: Health care services by a clinical establishment are exempt, subject to exceptions in the notification
Taxable at 18% with ITC
Taxable at 5% for all patients
Outside GST because hospitals are charitable
questions.explanation: Health care services by a clinical establishment are exempt under the services exemption notification. Exceptions exist (for example, certain non-ICU room rent above a per-day limit has been taxed); check the current notification. The hospital's exempt supplies restrict its ITC.

questions.prompt: What must the auditor do before using the valuation firm's VIU model?
options: Evaluate the expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity, agree the scope, and evaluate the adequacy of the work and its assumptions under SA 620
Accept the model as the expert is qualified
Refer to the expert in the audit opinion to share responsibility
Ask management to obtain a second valuation and use the average
questions.explanation: SA 620 requires the auditor to assess the expert's competence and objectivity, understand their field, agree the nature and scope of work, and evaluate the relevance and reasonableness of findings, assumptions and source data. The auditor keeps sole responsibility and does not refer to the expert in an unmodified report.

questions.prompt: In-process R&D acquired in a business combination is recognised as a separate intangible asset at fair value, even though similar internally generated research would be expensed.
questions.explanation: Ind AS 103 and Ind AS 38 treat acquired IPR&D as a separately identifiable asset with a fair value at acquisition. Subsequent research spend on it follows the normal Ind AS 38 rules.

questions.prompt: Which criteria must be demonstrated before development costs are capitalised under Ind AS 38?
options: Technical feasibility of completing the asset
Intention to complete and use or sell it
Availability of technical, financial and other resources to complete it
Ability to measure the expenditure reliably
Approval of the product by a foreign regulator
questions.explanation: Ind AS 38 lists six criteria, including the four selected plus ability to use or sell and probable future economic benefits. Regulatory approval is often the practical evidence in pharma but is not itself a listed criterion.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under Ind AS 36, recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and ___.
questions.explanation: Recoverable amount is the higher of FVLCD and value in use (the present value of future cash flows expected from the asset or CGU).

questions.prompt: Compute and allocate the impairment loss for SPL's US formulations CGU and pass the journal entry.
questions.data: Carrying amounts: goodwill ₹25 crore, plant ₹150 crore, ANDAs ₹75 crore. Value in use ₹210 crore; FVLCD ₹200 crore. No individual asset's FVLCD limits the allocation.
questions.answer:
**Recoverable amount** = higher of VIU 210 and FVLCD 200 = ₹210 crore. **Loss** = 250 - 210 = ₹40 crore.

| Asset | Carrying | Allocation | Revised |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Goodwill | 25 | 25 (first) | 0 |
| Plant and machinery | 150 | 15 x 150/225 = 10 | 140 |
| ANDAs | 75 | 15 x 75/225 = 5 | 70 |
| **Total** | **250** | **40** | **210** |

| Entry | Dr ₹ crore | Cr ₹ crore |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Impairment loss (P&L) Dr | 40 | |
| To Goodwill | | 25 |
| To Plant and machinery | | 10 |
| To Product intangibles | | 5 |

The goodwill impairment is never reversed; impairment of other assets may reverse if the warning letter is closed out. Disclose the event, key assumptions and sensitivity (Ind AS 36).

questions.prompt: Discuss the multidisciplinary impact of the USFDA warning letter on SPL.
questions.answer:
- **FR**: impairment of the US CGU (₹40 crore), NRV of US-bound inventory (Ind AS 2), provisions for remediation only when an obligation exists (Ind AS 37), disclosure of the event and its uncertainty.
- **Audit**: SA 250 (non-compliance with regulations), key audit matter on impairment (SA 701), SA 620 for the VIU model, SA 570 since 55% of revenue depends on the US.
- **AFM**: lower USD inflows change the hedging need; avoid over-hedging forecast sales that may not occur.
- **Law**: SEBI LODR requires prompt disclosure of the warning letter as material information.
- **SM**: weakness in the value chain (quality systems); options are remediation with consultants, shifting US filings to a second plant, and market development in other regulated markets to reduce concentration.

questions.prompt: Explain how SPL should decide between forward cover and a money market hedge for its USD receivable, and how it could account for the hedge.
questions.answer: Compare the rupee inflow at maturity: forward cover gives USD 20 million x 87.50 = ₹175.00 crore; the money market hedge gives about ₹174.24 crore, so the forward is better. The choice also depends on credit lines (the money market hedge uses a USD borrowing limit), counterparty risk and whether the receivable is certain. An option (USD put) costs a premium but keeps upside if the rupee weakens. Under Ind AS 109 SPL may designate the forward as a cash flow hedge of a highly probable forecast sale, with documentation of the risk management objective and effectiveness; gains and losses go to OCI and are reclassified when the sale affects profit. For a recognised receivable, the forward and the receivable's exchange differences offset in profit or loss without hedge accounting.

chapters.title: Case Set: Group Restructuring (Merger and Demerger)
chapters.summary: A group merges two fellow subsidiaries and demerges a division: swap ratios and EPS, Ind AS 103 common control accounting, tax neutrality conditions, cost of shares after demerger, GST on transfer of a going concern, NCLT schemes, fast-track mergers and portfolio strategy.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA; Companies Act 2013; SAs issued by ICAI; Income-tax Act 2025 (tax year 2026-27, Finance Act 2026); CGST/IGST Acts after the September 2025 rate rationalisation; Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations) Rules

lesson.heading: Merger valuation: swap ratio and EPS
lesson.body:
The swap (exchange) ratio is the number of acquirer shares issued for each target share. It is based on market price, EPS, net asset value, DCF, or a weighted mix, usually certified by a registered valuer (section 247 of the Companies Act).

| Measure | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Swap ratio (market price basis) | Target MPS / Acquirer MPS |
| Shares issued | Target shares x swap ratio |
| Post-merger EPS | (Acquirer earnings + target earnings + synergy) / (acquirer shares + shares issued) |
| Maximum ratio for no EPS dilution | ((Combined earnings / acquirer EPS) - acquirer shares) / target shares |
| EPS of target holders after merger | Post-merger EPS x swap ratio |

Worked check: if the acquirer P/E exceeds the target P/E and the ratio is based on market prices, the acquirer's EPS rises (bootstrapping) even without synergy. Explain that this gain is accounting, not value, unless synergies exist.

lesson.heading: Accounting: common control (Ind AS 103 Appendix C)
lesson.body:
When the combining entities are controlled by the same party before and after the combination (fellow subsidiaries, or a parent and subsidiary), Ind AS 103 Appendix C requires the **pooling of interests method**:

- Assets and liabilities are taken at their carrying amounts; no fair values and no new goodwill.
- The identity of reserves is preserved (general reserve stays general reserve).
- The difference between the share capital issued plus other consideration and the share capital of the transferor is transferred to **capital reserve**, shown separately.
- Prior period figures are restated as if the combination had occurred from the beginning of the preceding period (or from when common control began, if later).

A merger between unrelated parties uses the acquisition method instead: fair values, goodwill or bargain purchase gain.

lesson.heading: Tax neutrality of mergers and demergers
lesson.body:
The Income-tax Act 2025 carries forward the conditions of the 1961 Act (section numbers below are of the 1961 Act).

**Amalgamation** (section 2(1B)): all property and all liabilities of the amalgamating company pass to the amalgamated company, and shareholders holding at least three-fourths in value of the shares of the amalgamating company (other than shares already held by the amalgamated company) become its shareholders. Transfers are then not taxed as capital gains for the company or the shareholders (section 47(vi), (vii)). Accumulated losses and unabsorbed depreciation of the amalgamating company can be carried forward only if the section 72A conditions are met.

**Demerger** (section 2(19AA)): all property and liabilities of the undertaking transferred at book values, the resulting company issues shares to the demerged company's shareholders on a proportionate basis, shareholders holding at least three-fourths in value of the demerged company's shares become shareholders of the resulting company, and the undertaking is transferred as a going concern.

**Cost of shares after demerger** (sections 49(2C) and 49(2D)): cost of shares in the resulting company = original cost x net book value of assets transferred / net worth of the demerged company before demerger; the cost of the original shares is reduced by that amount.

**GST**: transfer of a business as a going concern (whole or an independent part) is an exempt service; unutilised ITC moves to the transferee under section 18(3) of the CGST Act (Form GST ITC-02).

lesson.heading: Company law: schemes of arrangement
lesson.body:
- Sections 230-232: application to the NCLT, meetings of shareholders and creditors (approval by majority representing three-fourths in value), notices to the Central Government (Regional Director), Registrar, income-tax authorities, RBI, SEBI and the stock exchanges, CCI and others as applicable.
- Objections to a scheme can be raised only by persons holding at least 10% of the shareholding or at least 5% of the total outstanding debt as per the latest audited financial statements (proviso to section 230(4)).
- No scheme is sanctioned unless the company's auditor certifies that the accounting treatment proposed in it conforms to the accounting standards under section 133.
- **Fast-track merger (section 233)**: available for mergers between two or more small companies, between a holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary, and other classes notified by the Central Government. It is approved by the Regional Director instead of the NCLT, after approval by members holding 90% of total shares and creditors representing nine-tenths in value.
- Listed companies also need stock exchange observation letters under SEBI's scheme framework.

lesson.heading: Strategy: why groups restructure
lesson.body:
- **Vertical integration** (merging a supplier into its customer) secures inputs and margins; horizontal mergers add scale and market share; conglomerate mergers diversify risk but can create a conglomerate discount.
- **Demerger and divestment**: separating a business with different growth, risk and capital needs lets each company attract the right investors, removes the conglomerate discount and sharpens management focus (BCG: separate the star from the cash cow).
- **Turnaround and retrenchment**: selling or closing dogs releases capital.

In the exam, pair the strategic rationale with the numbers: EPS accretion or dilution, synergy needed to justify the ratio, and the tax and legal route that keeps the restructuring tax-neutral.

keyPoints: Swap ratio (market basis) = target MPS / acquirer MPS; post-merger EPS = combined earnings / combined shares.
Common control: pooling of interests, carrying amounts, reserves preserved, difference to capital reserve.
Amalgamation and demerger: three-fourths in value of shareholders must become shareholders (sections 2(1B), 2(19AA) of the 1961 Act).
Cost after demerger = original cost x net book value transferred / net worth before demerger.
Transfer of a going concern is exempt from GST; ITC moves under section 18(3) via ITC-02.
Section 230(4): objections only from 10% shareholders or 5% debt holders; auditor's certificate on accounting treatment.
Section 233 fast track: small companies, holding and wholly owned subsidiary, and notified classes; approved by the Regional Director.

cases.title: Case: Bharat Diversified group - merger of Tarang into Aditya
cases.body:
Bharat Holdings Ltd (BHL) controls two listed subsidiaries: Aditya Industries Ltd (AIL), which makes packaging films, and Tarang Polymers Ltd (TPL), which makes polypropylene resin, about half of which is sold to AIL. BHL proposes to merge TPL into AIL with effect from 1 April 2027. Both companies follow Ind AS; both remain under BHL's control after the merger.

| Data | AIL | TPL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Profit after tax (₹ crore) | 300 | 60 |
| Number of shares (crore, face value ₹10) | 10 | 4 |
| Market price per share (₹) | 450 | 180 |

**TPL's balance sheet at the merger date (₹ crore)**: total assets 380; liabilities 160; share capital 40; general reserve 120; retained earnings 60.

The swap ratio will be based on market prices. Assume no synergy unless stated.

cases.title: Case: Bharat Diversified group - demerger of specialty chemicals
cases.body:
AIL also has a specialty chemicals division that grows at 20% a year but earns a low return now, while films are mature. Analysts value AIL at a discount to a sum-of-the-parts valuation. The board proposes to demerge the chemicals division into a new company, Aditya Specialty Ltd (ASL), which will issue one share for each AIL share and seek listing.

- Net book value of assets of the chemicals division: ₹300 crore. AIL's net worth immediately before the demerger: ₹1,200 crore.
- Meera, a shareholder, bought AIL shares at ₹500 each.
- AIL has unutilised ITC of ₹6 crore relating to the chemicals division.
- A minority shareholder group holding 4% of AIL's shares wants to object to the scheme before the NCLT.

questions.prompt: Compute the number of AIL shares to be issued to TPL's shareholders using the market price swap ratio. Answer in crore shares to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation:
Swap ratio = 180 / 450 = 0.4 AIL share for each TPL share (2 for 5).

Shares issued = 4 crore x 0.4 = **1.60 crore shares**.

questions.prompt: Compute AIL's EPS after the merger, assuming no synergy. Answer in ₹ to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: Post-merger EPS = (300 + 60) / (10 + 1.60) = 360 / 11.60 = **₹31.03**, against ₹30.00 before. EPS rises because AIL's P/E (450/30 = 15) is higher than TPL's (180/15 = 12); this is bootstrapping, not value creation.

questions.prompt: Compute the maximum swap ratio AIL can offer without diluting its pre-merger EPS. Answer to 2 decimals (AIL shares per TPL share).
questions.explanation: For EPS to stay at ₹30: total shares = 360 / 30 = 12 crore. Shares that can be issued = 12 - 10 = 2 crore. Maximum ratio = 2 / 4 = **0.50**.

questions.prompt: Under Ind AS 103 Appendix C, compute the capital reserve AIL records on the merger. Answer in ₹ crore.
questions.explanation:
Share capital issued = 1.60 crore shares x ₹10 = ₹16 crore. TPL's share capital = ₹40 crore.

Capital reserve = 40 - 16 = **₹24 crore**. TPL's general reserve (₹120 crore) and retained earnings (₹60 crore) are carried over in the same form.

questions.prompt: From AIL's point of view, the merger with TPL is best described as:
options: Vertical merger (backward integration), securing AIL's resin supply
Horizontal merger of two competitors
Conglomerate merger of unrelated businesses
Reverse merger to obtain a listing
questions.explanation: TPL supplies resin, a key input, to AIL. Merging a supplier is backward vertical integration: it secures supply and captures the supplier's margin. Both companies are already listed, so it is not a reverse merger for listing.

questions.prompt: Compute the cost of acquisition of each ASL share received by Meera on the demerger. Answer in ₹.
questions.explanation: Cost of ASL share = cost of AIL share x net book value transferred / net worth before demerger = 500 x 300 / 1,200 = **₹125** (corresponds to section 49(2C) of the 1961 Act). Cost of the AIL share is reduced to 500 - 125 = ₹375 (section 49(2D)).

questions.prompt: Which condition must the demerger meet for it to be tax-neutral?
options: Shareholders holding at least three-fourths in value of AIL's shares become shareholders of ASL
ASL must pay cash consideration to AIL equal to fair value
Only the assets, not the liabilities, of the division are transferred
ASL must be a wholly owned subsidiary of AIL
questions.explanation: Section 2(19AA) of the 1961 Act (carried forward in the 2025 Act) requires transfer of all property and liabilities of the undertaking at book values, proportionate issue of shares to AIL's shareholders, at least three-fourths in value of shareholders becoming ASL shareholders, and transfer as a going concern. Cash consideration to the company would defeat it.

questions.prompt: What is the GST position of the transfer of the chemicals division and its ₹6 crore unutilised ITC?
options: Transfer of a going concern is an exempt service; the ITC is transferred to ASL under section 18(3) by filing ITC-02
GST at 18% on the net book value of ₹300 crore
The ITC lapses on demerger
GST applies only to the movable assets transferred
questions.explanation: Services by way of transfer of a going concern, as a whole or an independent part, are exempt. Section 18(3) of the CGST Act allows unutilised ITC to be transferred to the transferee where there is a change in constitution due to demerger or transfer of business, with liabilities transferred specifically; Form GST ITC-02 is filed.

questions.prompt: Can the shareholder group holding 4% of AIL's shares object to the scheme before the NCLT?
options: No: objections may be made only by persons holding at least 10% of the shareholding or 5% of the total outstanding debt
Yes: any shareholder may object
Yes, if it holds at least 2%
No: only creditors can object to a demerger
questions.explanation: The proviso to section 230(4) restricts objections to persons holding not less than 10% of the shareholding or having outstanding debt of not less than 5% of total outstanding debt as per the latest audited financial statements. The group can still vote at the meeting and seek redress through other means such as SEBI.

questions.prompt: What is the main strategic rationale for the demerger?
options: Unlocking value by removing the conglomerate discount and letting each business attract investors suited to its growth and risk
Avoiding audit of the chemicals division
Increasing AIL's EPS by moving profits
Reducing the number of shareholders
questions.explanation: Chemicals is a high-growth, low-return business (a question mark or star in BCG terms) inside a mature films company (cash cow). Separately listed, each gets its own valuation, capital structure and management focus; the sum-of-the-parts discount should narrow.

questions.prompt: The amalgamated company can always carry forward and set off the accumulated business losses of the amalgamating company, whatever its line of business.
questions.explanation: Carry forward is allowed only where the amalgamating company owns an industrial undertaking (or other specified business) and the conditions of section 72A of the 1961 Act are met: for example, minimum years of business and asset holding by the amalgamating company, and the amalgamated company holding the assets and continuing the business for five years.

questions.prompt: Which mergers can use the fast-track route under section 233 of the Companies Act?
options: Between two or more small companies
Between a holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary
Other classes of companies notified by the Central Government
Between any two unrelated listed companies
questions.explanation: Section 233 covers small companies, a holding company with its wholly owned subsidiary, and classes notified by the Central Government (start-ups and certain other unlisted classes have been notified). Unrelated listed companies go through the NCLT route under sections 230-232.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: under Ind AS 103 Appendix C, business combinations of entities under common control are accounted for using the ___ method.
questions.explanation: Appendix C requires the pooling of interests method: carrying amounts, preserved reserves, and the share capital difference to capital reserve.

questions.prompt: Pass the journal entry in AIL's books to record the merger of TPL under the pooling of interests method.
questions.data: TPL at the merger date (₹ crore): total assets 380; liabilities 160; share capital 40; general reserve 120; retained earnings 60. AIL issues 1.6 crore equity shares of ₹10 each to TPL's shareholders.
questions.answer:
**Journal entry in AIL's books (₹ crore)**

| Entry | Dr | Cr |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assets of TPL (at carrying amounts) Dr | 380 | |
| To Liabilities of TPL | | 160 |
| To Equity share capital (1.6 crore x ₹10) | | 16 |
| To General reserve | | 120 |
| To Retained earnings | | 60 |
| To Capital reserve (40 - 16) | | 24 |
| **Total** | **380** | **380** |

Notes: no goodwill is recognised and assets are not fair valued. Intra-group balances (resin sales to AIL, payables and receivables) are eliminated and unrealised profit in AIL's inventory is removed. Comparatives are restated as if the merger had occurred from the beginning of the preceding period, as common control existed throughout. Disclose the capital reserve separately.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the statutory auditor in a scheme of merger or demerger?
questions.answer:
- Under the proviso to section 230(7) and section 232(3), the NCLT does not sanction a scheme unless the company's auditor certifies that the accounting treatment proposed in the scheme conforms to the accounting standards prescribed under section 133. The auditor checks the scheme's accounting clause against Ind AS 103 (Appendix C for common control) or the acquisition method.
- After sanction, the auditor audits the accounting in the year of the merger: appointed date vs effective date, Ind AS 10 if the NCLT order comes after year end, restated comparatives, elimination of intra-group items, and the capital reserve.
- The auditor considers related party aspects (SA 550), the valuer's report as management's expert, and subsequent events (SA 560).
- For listed companies, SEBI's scheme framework requires an auditor's certificate on the accounting treatment with the stock exchange filing.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the AIL-TPL merger from the viewpoint of AIL's and TPL's shareholders.
questions.answer:
- At the market-based ratio of 0.40, AIL's EPS rises from ₹30.00 to about ₹31.03, but only because AIL's P/E (15) exceeds TPL's (12); without synergy, this is bootstrapping.
- TPL holders get 0.40 x 31.03 = ₹12.41 of EPS per old share against ₹15.00 before, a fall; they accept because they share in AIL's higher multiple and any synergy.
- AIL can go up to a ratio of 0.50 without EPS dilution; the ratio of 0.40 leaves room for negotiation and a valuer's fairness opinion is needed.
- Real gains come from vertical integration: secure resin supply, removal of double margins and logistics savings.
- Risks: cyclical resin prices now fall on AIL's books; minority holders of both companies need fair treatment, and the auditor's certificate and NCLT approval are required before the merger takes effect.
